# Refusing the Impossible: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Code Hallucination in Large Language Models

- Authors: Dasu, Vishnu Asutosh; Kundu, Ashish; Tan, Gang
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint, not peer-reviewed)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2609.03267 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03267
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index); arXiv 2609.03267v2, 31 Oct 2026.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] Test whether code LLMs recognise programming requests that cannot be satisfied (nonexistent packages, impossible algorithms) and refuse; define code hallucination as ungrounded generation, distinct from code errors; provide a taxonomy and benchmark (p. 1, p. 2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1: How often do models comply with unsatisfiable requests rather than refuse, and is refusal a sign of over-caution? (p. 5)
- [A] RQ2: Does model scale reduce hallucination, equally for every kind? (p. 5)
- [A] RQ3: How do models hallucinate, and what failure modes do reasoning models add? (p. 5)
- [A] RQ4: What kinds of prompts exacerbate hallucination? (p. 5)

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Benchmark study with matched controls: unsatisfiable requests where any solution attempt is ungrounded by construction, plus minimal-edit solvable controls to detect over-refusal (p. 3, p. 4).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Taxonomy (Fig. 2): outcome CORRECT / HALLUCINATION / REFUSAL (ERROR on solvable tasks); D1 groundedness — absolute (A1–A4) vs relative (R1 nonexistent API or package, R2 header/flag, R3 protocol, R4 language feature, R5 fabricated version); D2 manifestation — syntactic / semantic / factual; D3 behaviour — B1 confident fabrication, B2 hedged compliance, B3 task substitution, B4 degenerate output (p. 3). Judge: Claude Opus 4.6 inside the Claude Code harness with a fixed rubric (six decision rules), shown prompt, response and ground-truth memo; responses that exhausted the token budget without an answer are labelled B4 by a deterministic rule (33 of 6,137) (p. 4). Hedged code counts as hallucination; fixing a typo and using the real package counts as correct (p. 4). An install/dependency line for a nonexistent name counts as using it (p. 4).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] 91 solvable controls (p. 4); comparison across 17 models and size groups (p. 5, p. 6).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] 270 hand-written adversarial templates, each with a memo naming the planted entity and why the request is unsatisfiable (e.g. crate `serde_ultra`) (p. 3, p. 4). Three families: theoretical impossibility (8 subcategories), plausible nonexistent entity (12, incl. nonexistent PyPI, npm, crates.io, Go, Java and C-header entities), typos/transplants/open tasks (4) (p. 4). Six languages: Python, C++, Rust, Go, Java, JavaScript (p. 4). Ten framing templates assigned by a hash of the seed, one frame per prompt (p. 4); Table VIII (p. 9).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 17 models x 361 prompts = 6,137 judged responses (p. 1, p. 2); 1,547 control responses (p. 2). Package subsets are small: 12 nonexistent-npm and 10 nonexistent-crate prompts (p. 9); subcategories have 6–20 prompts per model (p. 10).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Prompts hand-crafted; models chosen as open-weight, version-exact, with known parameter counts, covering small/older models still in production (p. 5).
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code artefacts and prompt suite open-sourced at a GitHub repository (rendered in the text layer as "https://github.com/vdasu/code hallucination") (p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Temperature 0, one completion per prompt, 16,384-token output budget; exception MiniMax-M2.7 at temperature 1.0, top-p 0.95 because it never left its reasoning phase under greedy decoding (p. 5). Models (Table III): DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B, CodeLlama 7B, CodeGemma 7B, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B, DeepCoder 14B, gpt-oss 20B, Devstral-Small-2 24B, Granite 4.1 30B, Qwen3-Coder 30B, Gemma 4 31B, Qwen2.5-Coder 32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill 32B, Qwen3-Coder-Next 80B, gpt-oss 120B, MiniMax-M2.7 230B, MiniMax-M3 428B, DeepSeek-V3.2 671B (p. 5). The twelve models up to 32B ran with 4-bit weight quantization, the five larger at full precision (p. 10). Re-run of 28 exhausted MiniMax-M3 prompts with a 131,072-token budget (p. 8). Inference engine, quantization method and hardware are not reported. How and when nonexistence of planted names was checked against registries is not described beyond the memo and the statement that relative prompts depend on registry state at generation time (p. 10).
- Code availability: [A] Yes (p. 2).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- [V] Hallucination rate (HR), refusal rate (RR), rate of correct non-refusals on adversarial prompts; over-refusal rate and HR on controls (p. 5).
- [V] 95% bootstrap intervals resampling prompts; Spearman correlation between log total parameters and HR (p. 5); Pearson correlation of adversarial vs control fabrication (p. 5); variance explained by prompt vs model identity (p. 8, p. 9).
- Judge validity: [V] on a 138-item gold set, outcome agreement 94%, Cohen's kappa 0.91; hallucination recall 0.93, precision 0.89; behaviour-label agreement 67%; manifestation 29/30, kappa 0.95; human labels replace judge labels for these 138 (p. 5).
- [V] No correction for multiple comparisons is reported in the metrics or results (p. 5, p. 6).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Across 17 models: 54% of responses to unsatisfiable prompts are ungrounded code, 31% refusals, 15% grounded non-refusals; only 1 of 1,547 control responses is a wrongful refusal; 5% of control responses hallucinate (p. 5).
2. [V] HR ranges from 0.23 (MiniMax-M3 428B) to 0.90 (CodeLlama 7B); small 4-bit models: CodeGemma 7B 0.84, Qwen2.5-Coder 7B 0.69, DeepSeek-Coder 6.7B 0.66, Table IV (p. 6).
3. [V] Scale helps on theoretical impossibilities (HR 0.84 / 0.49 / 0.32 for <=7B / 14–32B / >=80B; Spearman -0.71, p = 0.002) but much less on plausible nonexistent entities (0.88 / 0.71 / 0.61; -0.47, p = 0.059) and least on nonexistent npm packages + Rust crates (1.00 / 0.90 / 0.85; -0.43, p = 0.083); the size groups contain 4 small, 8 mid and 5 large models, Table V (p. 6). [I] The npm+crates subset has 22 prompts per model, so 1.00, 0.90 and 0.85 rest on 88, 176 and 110 responses respectively.
4. [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B) and gpt-oss 120B fabricate on 100% of nonexistent npm/crate prompts; gpt-oss 20B and 120B have the same overall HR (0.46) (p. 6).
5. [V] By ecosystem (pooled): nonexistent npm packages fabricated on 94% of prompts, Rust crates 87%, C headers 76%, Go modules 63%, PyPI modules 63%, Java APIs 33%; largest models 87%, 84%, 68%, 50%, 50%, 15% (p. 8).
6. [V] A misspelled real package name is fabricated on only 14% of prompts, versus 94% for a correctly spelled fictional one (p. 8, p. 9); responses that fix the typo and use the real package count as correct (p. 4).
7. [V] Behaviour: 66% confident fabrication (B1), 19% hedged (B2), 13% task substitution (B3), 1.5% degenerate (B4) (p. 6, p. 7). Manifestation: 47% semantic (would fail at install/import/compile), 43% factual (runs; only claims are false); 18% of plausible-entity hallucinations are factual (p. 7); Table VII (p. 8). [A] "no registry check will notice" them (p. 7).
8. [V] Framing matters: "internal docs" frame HR 0.64 vs "learner" 0.43; the docs vs question-frames gap is 21 points (95% CI 8–34) (p. 8); Table VIII (p. 9).
9. [V] Prompt identity explains 34% of outcome variance vs 15% for model identity; 33 of 270 prompts fool at least 16 of 17 models and 11 fool all 17 (p. 8, p. 9).
10. [V] Collision example: MiniMax-M2.7 recommended `pip install pywfm`, a name that exists on PyPI as an unrelated 2015 package (p. 9).
11. [V] MiniMax-M3 exhausted the 16,384-token budget on 28 of 361 prompts; with 131,072 tokens 23 finished and 5 still produced no answer (p. 8).
12. [A] Recommended mitigations: ground generation in package registries at generation time; gate output on the model's own stated caveats; ask the feasibility question before the implementation question (p. 9, p. 11).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Template-rendered prompts may differ from what developers type; absolute rates are benchmark-specific (p. 10).
- [A] Single sample per prompt; MiniMax-M2.7 run at temperature 1.0 (p. 10).
- [A] Relative prompts depend on the state of package registries at generation time; MiniMax-M2.7 has since been withdrawn (p. 10).
- [A] The LLM judge is the main internal threat; gold set labelled by one author; the judge sees the ground-truth memo, which could bias it (p. 10).
- [A] Models <=32B ran 4-bit, larger ones full precision: size is confounded with precision (p. 10).
- [A] Framing analysis is observational (one frame per prompt); subcategory counts are 6–20 per model, so the scale trend on plausible entities is treated as weak (p. 10).
- [A] Open-weight models only; may not generalise to closed frontier models (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] Construct differs from the slopsquatting threat model: the user supplies the fictional package name, so the benchmark measures *acceptance* of a planted name, not spontaneous invention of names. Rates such as 94% for npm (p. 8) are not comparable with spontaneous package hallucination rates from prompt-sampling studies.
- [I] Package-specific estimates rest on 22 prompts (12 npm + 10 crates, p. 9); per-model package rates have wide uncertainty (not reported per subcategory).
- [I] Publishing the planted fictional names creates a risk that someone registers them, silently changing ground truth for future replications (registry dependence acknowledged, p. 10).
- [I] Quantization method/engine and hardware not reported, which limits exact replication of the 4-bit small-model results.
- [I] Behaviour-level labels have only 67% judge-human agreement (p. 5); B1/B2 shares are indicative.
- [I] Very recent preprint (v2, 31 Oct 2026), not peer-reviewed.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: judge sees the memo; gold set from one author (p. 10); deterministic B4 rule affects 33 responses (p. 4) — [I].
- External: open-weight models only; template prompts (p. 10) — [I].
- Construct: "hallucination" includes hedged compliance (p. 4); planted-name acceptance vs spontaneous invention — [I].
- Statistical conclusion: bootstrap CIs given for model-level HR, Table IV (p. 6), and framing (p. 9); per-subcategory n = 6–20 (p. 10); size/precision confound (p. 10) — [I].
- Reproducibility: prompts, decoding and model identifiers reported; code released (p. 2, p. 5); engine/quantization method missing — [I].

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: registry grounding at generation time and caveat-gating tools; asking feasibility first; treating an exhausted reasoning budget as an impossibility signal (p. 9, p. 10, p. 11).
- Suggested by us [I]: evaluate a registry-check tool as an intervention on the npm/crate/PyPI subsets; add closed models and agentic tools; combine planted-name prompts with spontaneous-invention prompts in one design.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - RQ1: Across 17 open models, fabrication of nonexistent packages barely falls with scale; npm and Rust are worst, PyPI and Go intermediate, Java lowest (p. 6, p. 8). Small 4-bit models (6.7–7B) hallucinate on 66–90% of all unsatisfiable prompts (p. 6, p. 10).
  - RQ2: Collisions with unrelated real packages occur (`pywfm`, p. 9) — evidence that invented names can already be taken. Cross-model agreement (33/270 prompts fool >=16/17 models, p. 9) concerns names planted by the prompt, so it is not evidence of spontaneous name repetition.
  - RQ3: Recommends registry grounding and caveat-gating but does not evaluate them (p. 9). The 18% "factual" plausible-entity hallucinations (p. 7) install no fictitious package, so they do not bear on slopsquatting defences.
  - RQ4: Matched solvable controls and a validated LLM judge are useful design elements; the registry-state dependence is a known pitfall (p. 5, p. 10).
  - Laptop-scale implication: the benchmark is small (361 prompts) and public, and its small models were already run 4-bit (p. 10), the regime a laptop uses. A laptop study could re-run the npm/crate/PyPI/Go subsets on local 7B models in hours, and measure how much a simple install-time registry check (or a "does this package exist?" pre-prompt) reduces harm.
  - Replication checklist: temperature 0, single completion, 16,384 output tokens; 10 framing templates; judge rubric with memo; HR/RR/over-refusal with bootstrap CIs over prompts; Spearman vs log parameters (p. 4, p. 5).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | 17 open models write ungrounded code for 54% of unsatisfiable requests (HR 0.23–0.90 per model); only 1/1,547 control responses is a wrongful refusal | 5, 6 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ1 | Scale cuts fabrication of theoretical impossibilities (0.84->0.32) but barely of nonexistent packages/APIs (0.88->0.61); npm+crates 1.00->0.85 | 6 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ1 | When a nonexistent package is named in the prompt, models fabricate it for npm 94%, Rust crates 87%, Go 63%, PyPI 63%, Java 33% | 8 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ1 | Request framing as routine work raises HR by 21 points vs question framing (95% CI 8–34) | 8, 9 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ1 | Small models (<=32B) were evaluated at 4-bit; 7B models hallucinate on 66–90% of unsatisfiable prompts | 6, 10 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ1 | 33 of 270 prompts fool at least 16 of 17 models; prompt identity explains 34% of outcome variance vs 15% for model. [I] Names are supplied by the prompt; not evidence of spontaneous cross-model repetition | 8, 9 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ2 | A hallucinated install name (`pywfm`) collides with an unrelated existing PyPI package | 9 | [V] | weak |
| RQ2 | A misspelled real package name is fabricated on 14% of prompts (vs 94% for correctly spelled fictional names); the rest are corrected or refused | 4, 8 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ3 | Authors recommend registry grounding at generation time and gating output on the model's own caveats (not evaluated) | 9, 11 | [A] | weak |
| RQ3 | [V] 18% of plausible-entity hallucinations are factual (real code, false claims). [A] "no registry check will notice" them. [I] These responses install no fictitious package, so they do not bear on slopsquatting defences | 7 | [V] | weak |
| RQ4 | LLM judge (Claude Opus 4.6) agrees with human labels on 94% of outcomes (kappa 0.91) but only 67% of behaviour labels | 5 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ4 | Results depend on registry state at generation time; size confounded with 4-bit quantization | 10 | [A] | moderate |
| RQ5 | Closed frontier models and agentic settings are not evaluated | 10 | [A] | moderate |

# LLM Hallucinations in Practical Code Generation: Phenomena, Mechanism, and Mitigation

- Authors: Zhang, Ziyao; Wang, Chong; Wang, Yanlin; Shi, Ensheng; Ma, Yuchi; Zhong, Wanjun; Chen, Jiachi; Mao, Mingzhi; Zheng, Zibin
- Year / venue: 2025, Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (published) — vol. 2, ISSTA issue, pp. 481–503 as cited in [@zheng2026when, p. 11]; also cited as ISSTA 2025 in [@dasu2026refusing, p. 11]. Not FSE.
- DOI: 10.1145/3728894 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3728894
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The text is the arXiv copy (2409.20550v2, 17 Jan 2025), not the published version; its author list has five authors (Zhang, Wang Y., Wang C., Chen, Zheng) (p. 1) versus nine in the published metadata, so content may differ from the PACMSE version.

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

## 1. Research objective
[A] Study the phenomena, mechanism and mitigation of LLM hallucinations in practical, repository-level code generation, going beyond standalone-function benchmarks (p. 1).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- [A] RQ1 (Taxonomy): What are the manifestations of hallucinations in practical code generation, and how are they distributed? (p. 1)
- [A] RQ2 (LLM comparison): How do LLMs compare in hallucination occurrences and patterns? (p. 1)
- [A] RQ3 (Root causes): What are the root causes? (p. 1)
- [A] Plus an exploratory RAG-based mitigation (p. 2, p. 9). No hypotheses.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Qualitative open coding of generated code to build a taxonomy, followed by descriptive distribution analysis and a pilot mitigation experiment (p. 3, p. 9).
- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Open coding: 10% of the 230 CoderEval Python tasks (23 tasks) x 6 models x 10 samples = 1,380 snippets; each snippet tested in the task's real environment; two authors compare with the ground truth and record hallucinations; a preliminary taxonomy is formed; remaining snippets annotated independently by three volunteers (two with >10 years, one with 4 years of Python experience), with new types discussed (p. 3). Model outputs were mixed before annotation and one author reviewed all labels (p. 10). Mitigation: RepoCoder-style retrieval corpus per repository using a sliding window of 20 lines and step 2, excluding ground-truth lines to prevent leakage; sparse bag-of-words with Jaccard similarity; top-10 snippets added to the prompt (p. 9).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] "Raw" prompting with docstring and function signature only (p. 9).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s): [V] CoderEval Python: 230 tasks from real repositories, each with description, ground-truth code, tests and project environment (p. 3).
- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 6 models x 10 snippets per task (p. 3); 13,800 snippets in total by our computation (230 x 6 x 10) — the paper does not state the total or the number of hallucination instances in the text (Fig. 2 and Fig. 11 show distributions, p. 4, p. 8).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Random selection of the 23 seed tasks (p. 3); all models generate for all tasks.
- Data availability (public? link?): [A] Code, data and results at https://github.com/DeepSoftwareAnalytics/LLMCodingHallucination (p. 1, p. 2).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo, CodeGen-350M-Mono, PanGu-alpha-2.6B, DeepSeekCoder-6.7B base, CodeLlama-7b-Python-hf, StarCoder2-7B (p. 3). Nucleus sampling, temperature 0.6, 10 samples per task, following CoderEval (p. 3). Hardware, max tokens and exact prompt templates are not reported.
- Code availability: [A] Yes (p. 1).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- [V] Percentage of hallucination instances per category/type (p. 4–p. 7); a snippet can contain several hallucinations (p. 3).
- [V] Pass@1 on CoderEval tests for the mitigation (p. 9).
- Statistical testing: [V] none; no inter-rater reliability statistic (p. 10).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] Taxonomy of 3 categories and 8 types, Fig. 1 (p. 4): Task Requirement Conflicts 43.53% (functional 36.66%, non-functional 6.86%) (p. 4, p. 5); Factual Knowledge Conflicts 31.91% (background 8.82%, library 2.68%, API 20.41%) (p. 5, p. 6); Project Context Conflicts 24.56% (environment 0.94%, dependency 11.26%, non-code resource 12.36%) (p. 6, p. 7).
2. [V] The package-existence case appears under Environment Conflicts: CodeGen imports `_lfu_cache`, a package that does not exist in the current environment (p. 6, p. 7). Environment Conflicts also cover version mismatches of platforms, languages and libraries (p. 6). [I] `_lfu_cache` is not a valid PyPI distribution name under PEP 508 (names must start with a letter or digit), so it is most likely a missing internal module, not a slopsquatting target; the 0.94% Environment Conflicts share is therefore an upper bound on invented-package cases.
3. [V] Dependency Conflicts are mostly non-existent project-internal functions/attributes (e.g. a similar-but-wrong function name) (p. 6, p. 7); API Knowledge Conflicts include non-existent parameters of real APIs (e.g. `timedelta(year=1)`) (p. 6).
4. [V] Security-relevant non-functional example: generated code uses `yaml.load` instead of `safe_load` (p. 5).
5. [V] Task Requirement Conflicts are the most frequent category for all six models; CodeGen and StarCoder2 have notably more, DeepSeekCoder and CodeLlama fewer; PanGu-alpha has the most factual-knowledge conflicts (p. 8).
6. [A] Four root causes: training-data quality, intention understanding, knowledge acquisition, repository-level context awareness (p. 8, p. 9).
7. [V] RAG mitigation raises Pass@1 for all models: CodeGen 1.30% -> 2.61%, PanGu-alpha 0.04% -> 1.74%, DeepSeekCoder 3.04% -> 3.91%, CodeLlama 2.17% -> 5.22%, StarCoder2 0.04% -> 2.61%, ChatGPT 10.40% -> 12.61%, Table I (p. 9). [A] The improvement is modest and the study is a pilot (p. 9).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Python only; CoderEval has only 230 tasks (mitigated by 6 models x 10 samples) (p. 10).
- [A] No formal inter-rater reliability measure; disagreements resolved in meetings; one author reviewed all labels (p. 10).
- [A] Possible model bias in annotation, mitigated by mixing outputs (p. 10).
- [A] Mitigation evaluated with CoderEval test cases (p. 10); retrieval corpus limited to the current repository, insufficient for background-knowledge conflicts (p. 10).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] The mitigation is evaluated by Pass@1, not by hallucination counts (p. 9), so the paper gives no direct evidence that RAG reduces hallucinations, and none for package hallucination specifically.
- [I] No registry (PyPI) check: "non-existent package" means not available in the task's environment (p. 6), so invented PyPI names cannot be separated from real but uninstalled packages.
- [I] Category shares are shares of hallucination instances with no stated totals or per-model denominators in the text (p. 4), so per-sample rates cannot be derived.
- [I] Models are dated and small (CodeGen-350M, PanGu-alpha-2.6B, GPT-3.5) (p. 3); Pass@1 values as low as 0.04% (p. 9) suggest near-total failure of some base models in this setting.
- [I] Version mismatch: we analysed the arXiv v2 text, which lists five authors (p. 1) while the published metadata lists nine; other project papers cite it as the ISSTA 2025 issue of PACMSE [@zheng2026when, p. 11; @dasu2026refusing, p. 11], not FSE.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: annotation without IRR (p. 10); taxonomy built from the same data it is applied to — [I].
- External: Python, one benchmark, 2023-era models (p. 3, p. 10) — [I].
- Construct: Pass@1 as a proxy for hallucination mitigation (p. 9) — [I].
- Statistical conclusion: no tests or uncertainty (p. 9) — [I].
- Reproducibility: replication package available (p. 1); prompts and hardware not in the paper — [I].

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]: hallucination identification and localisation techniques; richer RAG sources (search engines, API documentation, Stack Overflow); input query refinement; multi-agent systems with tools (search, static analysis); fine-tuning (p. 9, p. 10); taxonomies for other languages (p. 10).
- Suggested by us [I]: re-annotate with a registry check to measure how many environment/library conflicts are invented PyPI names.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ1 (marginal), RQ3 (background), RQ4 (background).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - Mainly background: places package hallucination inside a broader taxonomy of code hallucination (Project Context / Environment and Factual Knowledge / Library-API conflicts) (p. 4).
  - RQ1: In repository-level Python completion with these models, missing-package/environment problems are a very small share (0.94%) of all hallucination instances (p. 6) — a different setting from prompt-to-code studies that ask for whole programs.
  - RQ3: Repository-context RAG is a cheap baseline but was not shown to reduce hallucinations directly (p. 9).
  - Laptop-scale implication: all open models used are <=7B and runnable locally, and CoderEval is small; but the study gives little for a package-hallucination measurement or defence. Cite as related-work context only.
  - Replication checklist: CoderEval Python (230 tasks), 10 samples, nucleus sampling temperature 0.6; RAG window 20 lines, step 2, BOW-Jaccard, top-10 snippets; Pass@1 (p. 3, p. 9).

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | In repository-level Python generation (CoderEval, 6 LLMs <=7B + GPT-3.5), Environment Conflicts (incl. importing a non-existent package) are 0.94% of hallucination instances, vs 20.41% API Knowledge Conflicts. [I] The only example (`_lfu_cache`) is not a valid PyPI name (PEP 508), so 0.94% is an upper bound on invented-package cases | 6 | [V] | weak |
| RQ3 | Repository-context RAG (BOW-Jaccard, top-10 snippets) raises Pass@1 for all 6 models by 0.87–3.05 points; effect on hallucination counts not measured | 9 | [V] | weak |
| RQ4 | Taxonomy: 3 categories / 8 types; package-related errors fall under Environment (Project Context) and Library/API (Factual Knowledge) conflicts | 4 | [V] | moderate |
| RQ4 | Manual annotation without a formal inter-rater reliability measure | 10 | [A] | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "attempts to use the package _lfu_cache, which does not exist in the current environment" (p. 6)
> "A key issue is the absence of formal inter-rater reliability measure for annotating hallucinations." (p. 10)
> "Note that the performance improvement in our experiments is modest" (p. 9)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: whole paper read (pp. 1–10 text; pp. 11–13 references skimmed). Figures 2 and 11 are charts without numeric labels in the text layer; shares taken from section text.
- Uncertainties: We analysed arXiv v2 (5 authors). An OA published version (9 authors) exists via the metadata oa_pdf_url (https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3728894) but was not analysed and may differ. Total number of hallucination instances not reported in the text.

# Library Hallucinations in LLM-Generated Code: A Risk Analysis Grounded in Developer Queries

- Authors: Twist, Lukas; Harman, Mark; Yannakoudakis, Helen; Zhang, Jie M.
- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (published)
- DOI: 10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.78 · URL: https://doi.org/10.18653/2026.emnlp-main.78
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

**Source tier:** Tier 1, peer-reviewed: EMNLP 2026 main conference, pp. 1785–1812 (p. 1).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] The authors present "the first systematic study of how user-level prompt variations influence library hallucinations" (p. 1). It covers two kinds:
  - library *name* hallucinations (invalid imports);
  - library *member* hallucinations (invalid calls from valid libraries).
- [A] They also aim to provide a reproducible benchmark, LibHalluBench, built from the highest-risk conditions (pp. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No numbered RQs. The paper runs two main experiments (pp. 3–4):
  - **Exp. 1, user language.** Do realistic library descriptions mined from StackExchange (e.g. "fast", "modern", "from 2025") change hallucination rates?
  - **Exp. 2, user mistakes.** Do one-character typos, multi-character typos, or fake names/members cause hallucinations?
- Additional studies (pp. 7–8):
  - prompt engineering;
  - other ecosystems (JavaScript, Rust);
  - rarity-seeking language;
  - access to a PyPI-existence tool;
  - ablations and controls.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Controlled experiments that change one prompt slot (`{library directive}`) in a fixed template. Each condition is measured across seven LLMs with three responses per prompt (pp. 3–4, 15).
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - [V] **Extraction.** Code blocks are found by regex. Python's `ast` module then reads import statements (handling aliases and namespace packages) and function/attribute calls (p. 4).
  - [V] **Name check.** Names are compared with PyPI after PyPA name normalisation (p. 4).
    - Manual validation found import names that differ from PyPI names (e.g. `python-dateutil` imported as `dateutil`); these were corrected (p. 15).
    - The one remaining false positive was `pywintypes`, "not directly available as a standalone PyPI package" (p. 15).
    - [I] PyPA normalisation only folds case and treats `-`, `_` and `.` as equivalent (general packaging knowledge). It cannot map `dateutil` → `python-dateutil` or `cv2` → `opencv-python`.
    - [I] The check therefore mainly tests whether the *import name* exists on PyPI. An import name that someone else has registered on PyPI counts as valid. Apart from the hand-corrected cases, a correct import whose name is not registered would count as a hallucination.
  - [V] **Member check.** Members are compared with scraped official documentation for the latest library version (pp. 4–5).
  - [V] **Version exclusion.** Responses that state a valid explicit version are excluded (p. 5).
  - [V] **Generated mistakes.** Typos and fake names are generated by o4-mini. Edit distance is checked (1, or 2–8), and every name is verified to be non-existent (pp. 4, 17).
- Baselines or comparison conditions (pp. 5–6, 18, 21): [V]
  - the "No description" condition (Exp. 1);
  - the "None, valid library/member" condition (Exp. 2);
  - unprompted vs prompt-engineered vs tool-augmented runs.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s):
  - [V] **BigCodeBench** (1,140 tasks), filtered to tasks that do not name the ground-truth library and whose libraries have accessible documentation (p. 3).
    - This leaves 356 tasks using 30 libraries; 10% are held out for preliminary experiments (p. 3).
    - LibHalluBench is built from the 321 remaining seed tasks (p. 8).
  - [V] **Software Recommendations StackExchange.** Over 20,000 questions were filtered to 3,917 library-related ones and clustered into nine descriptors. 23 question titles contain a year (pp. 4, 16).
  - [V] **CodeInsight test split** (1,860 records). The longest 50% were kept, 500 sampled, and an LLM rewrote them to be independent of any library or language (p. 19).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] Three responses per prompt (p. 4).
  - [V] Two instances of each error type per task (p. 4).
  - [V] Ecosystem study (pp. 7, 20):
    - The paper states each model generated "one response per task" (p. 20).
    - The Python and JavaScript rates in Table 5 move in 0.20% steps, consistent with one response for each of the 500 tasks (p. 20).
    - The study covers 140 Python, 161 JavaScript and 184 Rust libraries.
- Sampling / selection method:
  - [V] The StackExchange filter was validated on 200 hand-labelled questions (precision and recall 0.95) (p. 15).
  - [V] A cluster was kept only if it linked to at least 20 questions (p. 16).
- Data availability:
  - [V] Code and full model outputs are on GitHub (p. 2).
  - [V] LibHalluBench is on Hugging Face (gated access) and on PyPI (`libhallubench`), with a canary string (pp. 8, 23).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] **Models, with exact versions** (p. 15):

    | Model | Version | Temperature | top_p |
    |---|---|---|---|
    | GPT-4o-mini | gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
    | GPT-5-mini | gpt-5-mini-2025-08-07 | 1.0 | 1.0 |
    | Ministral-8B | ministral-2410 | 0.3 | 1.0 |
    | Qwen-2.5-Coder | qwen2.5-coder-32b-instruct | 0.7 | 0.8 |
    | Llama-3.3 | llama-3.3-70b-instruct-turbo | 0.6 | 0.9 |
    | DeepSeek-V3.1 | deepseek-chat-v3.1 | 0.6 | 0.5 |
    | Claude-4.5-Haiku | claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 | 1.0 | 1.0 |

  - [V] All models are accessed through provider APIs (OpenAI, Mistral, Together, DeepSeek, Anthropic). Each call is a fresh session with no system prompt (p. 3).
  - [V] Model information was recorded as of "the time of the study (January 2026)" (p. 15).
  - [V] DeepSeek-V3.1 was replaced by V3.2 for the ecosystem and ablation runs (p. 14).
  - [V] **Registries and snapshots.**
    - Python names are checked against PyPI (p. 4), and the tool study used a "cached PyPI package list" (p. 22); the snapshot date is not reported.
    - JavaScript names are checked against the all-the-package-names list (jsDelivr, 2026); Rust names against Cargo's registry (p. 20). Neither snapshot is dated.
    - The only dated snapshot is the top-1,000 most-downloaded PyPI packages (January 2026). It was used to filter CodeInsight tasks that name known libraries (p. 19).
  - Hardware: not reported (API-only).
- Code availability: [V] GitHub repository (pp. 2, 23).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] **RHR:** share of responses containing a hallucination.
  - [V] **THR:** share of tasks where at least one of the three responses hallucinates (p. 5).
  - [V] **Tool study:** hallucination rate, share of responses using the tool, tool calls per response, and share of responses with no code (p. 21).
  - [V] **Detector validation:** precision and recall on 200 high-risk responses (pp. 5, 15).
  - [V] In Exp. 2, for valid names, the rate shown is how often the requested valid library was *not* used (p. 6).
- Statistical testing: none reported (no tests, CIs or effect sizes). "Significantly" is used descriptively (pp. 6, 8).

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] **Normal prompts rarely produce invented library names.** With "No description" and the adjective prompts, library-name RHR is ≤0.31% for every model (p. 5).
2. [V] **Year-based prompts drive library-name hallucination.** "From 2025" THR by model (p. 5):
   - GPT-4o-mini 84.74%
   - GPT-5-mini 63.86%
   - Qwen-2.5-Coder 61.68%
   - DeepSeek-V3.1 38.01%
   - Ministral-8B 32.40%
   - Llama-3.3 1.87%
   - Claude-4.5-Haiku 0.62%

   [V] Year control (p. 28):
   - "From 2022" stays below 1.1% RHR.
   - "From 2026" gives 59.81% for DeepSeek-V3.2 vs 0.73% for Claude.

   [A] Knowledge cut-off contributes to the effect but does not fully explain it (p. 28).
3. [V] **Models go along with user mistakes.** Library-name THR (p. 6):
   - one-character typos: up to 25.86% (GPT-5-mini);
   - multi-character typos: up to 79.44% (GPT-5-mini);
   - fake library names: 90.50–99.22% for GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5-mini and Ministral-8B, vs 20.72% for Qwen-2.5-Coder.

   [V] On average, fake members are used in 31% of tasks vs 69% for fake names (p. 7). [A] The authors link this to sycophancy and say LLMs "may amplify typosquatting risks" (pp. 2, 6).
4. [V] **Rarity-seeking language.** "Hidden gem" raises the average library-name THR to 5.35%, the highest of the adjective prompts (p. 8).
5. [V] **Prompt engineering is inconsistent** (pp. 18–19).
   - Self-analysis reduces hallucinations in 29/36 settings and explicit-check in 30/36.
   - Chain-of-thought and step-back are inconsistent. For example, Qwen-2.5-Coder's fake-name RHR rises by 28.66 points under chain-of-thought.
6. [V] **A PyPI-existence tool helps but does not remove the problem** (pp. 8, 21).
   - GPT-4o-mini calls it on 98.65% of "from 2025" responses and hallucinates in 2.49%.
   - GPT-5-mini calls it on only 7.89% and returns no code 90.76% of the time.
   - Under user mistakes, invalid libraries are still accepted in up to 38.79% of cases.
7. [V] **Other ecosystems** (CodeInsight, RHR; p. 20):
   - JavaScript: fake names 27.2–88.8%.
   - Rust: fake names 41.30–96.76%; "from 2025" up to 57.40% (Qwen).
8. [V] **Detector validation** (pp. 5, 15).
   - Of 24 automatically flagged responses, 23 were true hallucinations (95.8% precision).
   - No false negatives were found in the 200-response sample.
   - The one false positive was `pywintypes`.
9. [V] **LibHalluBench baselines** (overall task-level rate across the Describe and Specify splits; p. 23): Llama-3.3 is lowest at 10.4%; GPT-4o-mini (39.0%) and GPT-5-mini (39.8%) are highest.
10. [V] **Robustness.** Greedy decoding and typos generated by Qwen3-235B leave the qualitative patterns unchanged (pp. 26–27).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] **Generalisability.** A finite set of tasks, ecosystems and model versions. Behaviour may differ for other languages, domain frameworks, low-resource ecosystems or future models (p. 9).
- [A] **Internal validity.** Risks from automatic extraction and prompt construction are mitigated with unit tests and manual validation (pp. 9–10).
- [A] **External validity.** Dataset bias, and LLM nondeterminism and updates. Leakage, if any, would make the results conservative (p. 10).
- [A] Evolving models and package ecosystems may affect reproducibility (p. 10).
- [A] The prompt-engineering study is not exhaustive, and the tool study is a "small case study" on the GPT models only (pp. 7–8).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Exp. 2 measures compliance, not spontaneous invention.** The invalid name comes from the user's prompt, so an attacker cannot predict it from the model. This is a *typosquatting-amplification* threat model, not classic slopsquatting of names the model invents.
- [I] **Registered names count as valid.**
  - Generated mistakes were filtered to be *unregistered* (pp. 4, 17), and any name present on PyPI counts as valid (p. 4).
  - Hallucinations that collide with already-registered or squatted names are therefore invisible by design, which undercounts the real security risk.
- [I] **Import names are checked, not distribution names.**
  - PyPA normalisation cannot map import names to distribution names; only cases spotted by hand (e.g. `dateutil`) were corrected (p. 15).
  - So a third-party package registered under an import name counts as valid, and an unregistered import name of a real distribution may count as a hallucination.
  - raj2026names handles the same ambiguity the opposite way, flagging registered import names. Rates from the two papers are not comparable.
- [I] **Registry snapshots undated.** Neither the PyPI check in the main experiments (p. 4) nor the JavaScript and Rust lists (p. 20) have a reported snapshot date.
- [I] **Persistence not reported.** Whether the same invented names recur across runs or models is not reported, yet it is central for slopsquatting (RQ2).
- [I] **Small validation sample.** Detector precision rests on 24 flagged responses. Recall is inferred from 200 responses drawn from only two high-risk conditions (p. 15).
- [I] **Mixed temperatures.** Default temperatures differ across models (0.3–1.0; p. 15), which confounds model comparisons. The greedy-decoding ablation (p. 26) partly addresses this.
- [I] **No uncertainty reporting.** Differences such as 0.10% vs 0.31% amount to one response or one task.
- [I] **API models only.** No local or quantized models were tested.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal:
  - Year prompts are partly confounded with knowledge cut-off; the control study is small (p. 28).
  - LLM-generated typos may not match real human typos; the provider ablation mitigates this (p. 27).
- External:
  - The main results rest on one benchmark (BigCodeBench, 30 libraries) and single-turn, single-function prompts; there is no agentic setting.
  - The ecosystem study extends to JavaScript and Rust, with one response per task (p. 20).
- Construct:
  - "Hallucination" means "import name not on the registry, or member not in the docs".
  - Already-registered hallucinations and registered import names count as correct.
  - Compliance with user mistakes (Exp. 2) is labelled as hallucination.
- Statistical conclusion: no tests or CIs. Three responses per prompt limit per-task resolution.
- Reproducibility: strong. Versions, parameters, prompts, code, outputs and the benchmark are all released (pp. 2, 15–17, 23). The DeepSeek version had to be swapped (p. 14).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - models that are aware of their knowledge cut-off and resist sycophancy;
  - lightweight existence checks before a library is chosen;
  - reporting hallucination, refusal, tool-use and calibration metrics (p. 9);
  - more robust approaches: grounding, fine-tuning, architecture changes (p. 19);
  - agentic coding workflows (p. 9).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - measure whether invented names repeat, and how many are already registered;
  - run LibHalluBench on local quantized models;
  - compare a *forced*, client-side existence check with tools the model may choose to call;
  - use an explicit import→distribution mapping in the check.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids):
  - RQ1: drivers (prompt type, model, ecosystem).
  - RQ3: prompt-engineering and tool-use defences.
  - RQ4: name normalisation and its limits, version exclusion, detector validation, the benchmark.
  - RQ2: typosquat amplification (indirectly).
  - RQ5: untested settings (local/quantized models, agents, collisions with registered names).
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **A ready-made trigger set.**
    - LibHalluBench (4,173 prompts) and the `libhallubench` package give a trigger set that runs on a laptop.
    - Year-based and typo/fake-name prompts are the highest-yield conditions for a small measurement study.
  - **Untested setting.** Running the benchmark against local quantized open models (none were tested here) is an obvious, cheap extension.
  - **Why a forced check matters.**
    - The tool study shows that an existence check the model must choose to call depends on the model actually calling it; GPT-5-mini rarely did.
    - A *forced*, client-side check, as in raj2026names, removes that dependency. Comparing the two is a well-defined defence experiment.
  - **What to adopt for the method.**
    - Use name normalisation **plus an explicit import→distribution map**, since normalisation alone cannot resolve `dateutil`/`cv2`-type cases (p. 15).
    - Keep the version-exclusion rule.
    - Record "registered but suspicious" as its own status; this paper by design does not measure it.
  - **Evidence strength: moderate–strong.** Peer-reviewed, 7 models, repeated sampling and ablations, but no inferential statistics and the main results rest on one benchmark.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)

## 14. Key quotes
> "fabricated library names are accepted in up to 99%" (p. 1)

> "tool access alone is insufficient, as models must still decide when to invoke the tool and how to respond to failed checks" (p. 9)

> "any residual data leakage is likely to only cause fewer hallucinations, making our findings conservative" (p. 10)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 28 PDF pages (main text, limitations, Appendices A–G). Figure 1 (p. 2) is a pipeline diagram, used via its caption. The two-column text extraction interleaves columns; we checked table rows against their headers.
- Uncertainties:
  - No snapshot dates for PyPI, the npm list or the crates registry.
  - Standard-library exclusion is not stated explicitly.
  - The `metadata.json` abstract ends with stray text ("Augmentation.Northern"), an artefact of metadata resolution, not of the paper.
- Critical-review fixes (2026-11-12):
  - **Applied:**
    - limits of name normalisation and the import→distribution map (§3, §9, §12);
    - undated JavaScript/Rust registries, and the January 2026 snapshot correctly placed as the CodeInsight task filter (p. 19), not a rarity list (§5);
    - main finding now includes the 79.44% multi-character figure.
  - **Not applied:** the review asked to remove "one response per task" for the ecosystem study as unsupported. Page 20 states it verbatim ("with each model generating one response per task"), and Table 5's 0.20% steps match n = 500, so we kept it.

# An Empirical Analysis of Static Analysis Methods for Detection and Mitigation of Code Library Hallucinations

- Authors: Miranda-Pena, Clarissa; Reeson, Andrew; Paris, Cécile; Poon, Josiah; Kummerfeld, Jonathan K.
- Year / venue: 2026, arXiv (preprint)
- DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2604.07755 · URL: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.07755
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

**Source tier:** **Preprint (tier 3), not confirmed as peer-reviewed.**
- [A] The PDF header reads "Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (10/2026)". Page 1 gives "Reviewed on OpenReview" with a forum link, and the arXiv stamp is v3, 6 Nov 2026 (p. 1).
- `metadata.json` records `venue_kind: preprint`, and no TMLR DOI or OpenReview record has been verified.
- Orchestrator decision (2026-11-12): keep at preprint tier. TMLR acceptance is treated as an author claim.

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Quantify what static analysis can and cannot do to detect and mitigate *library hallucinations* in NL-to-code generation. A library hallucination is code that would only work if imagined libraries, functions, parameters or types existed (pp. 1, 3).
- [A] Establish an upper bound for static methods through manual analysis (pp. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs. The stated contributions are (p. 2):
  1. an analysis of static tools for detection and mitigation;
  2. manual hallucination annotations on three benchmarks;
  3. a docstring-to-grammar framework for constrained decoding.
- Implicit questions (pp. 5–11):
  - detection precision and recall (§5.1);
  - the upper bound, and the causes of misses (§5.1.1–5.1.2);
  - whether LLM repair guided by tool output fixes hallucinations (§5.2);
  - whether constrained decoding prevents them (§5.3).

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] A comparative empirical evaluation with four parts (pp. 4–11):
  - three detectors plus a baseline;
  - repair with and without tool output;
  - constrained vs unconstrained decoding;
  - manual annotation of a sample of failures.

  It runs on three execution-based benchmarks with six generation models.
- Approach / model / intervention:
  - [V] **(1) Grammar.** A GBNF grammar auto-extracted from library docstrings via `inspect` and combined with the Python grammar. It is used for post-hoc checks and for constrained decoding in llama.cpp/Ollama. Its import rule validates packages "in the environment of the benchmark and Python built-in modules" (pp. 3–4).
  - [V] **(2) Off-the-shelf analysers.** Mypy and Pyright, with auto-generated type stubs (p. 4).
  - [V] **(3) Baseline judge.** o3-mini as an LLM judge, asked whether the code will execute (p. 4).
  - [V] **Repair.** o3-mini is given the code and the error, either alone ("o3+Self") or with Mypy/Pyright output (pp. 9–10).
- Baselines or comparison conditions (pp. 6, 9, 11): [V]
  - detection: the o3-mini judge;
  - repair: "No repair" and o3+Self;
  - mitigation: unconstrained decoding.

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s) (p. 5): [V]
  - DS-1000: 1,000 problems, 7 libraries;
  - ODEX: 945 problems, 79 libraries, 4 natural languages;
  - BigCodeBench-instruct: 1,140 problems, 139 libraries.
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] All questions of DS-1000 and BigCodeBench, plus "550 questions from RIG"; questions not needing imports were skipped (p. 5). [I] "RIG" is never defined and is probably ODEX.
  - [V] Six generation models (p. 5).
  - [V] Manual analysis: 200 failure cases per benchmark, 600 in total, sampled equally across claude-3, gpt-3.5, gpt-4 and Granite 3B (p. 6).
  - [V] Repair: erroneous samples numbered 2,210 for DS-1000, 2,001 for BigCode and 1,291 for Odex (p. 10).
- Sampling / selection method:
  - [V] The benchmarks were chosen because they combine an NL prompt that demands library use with test cases (p. 5).
  - How the manual sample was drawn within the strata is not reported.
- Data availability:
  - [V] Benchmarks are used under Apache-2.0 / CC-BY-SA-4.0 (p. 17).
  - [A] The annotation guideline is supplemental material (pp. 7, 17).
  - Release of the generated outputs or annotations: not reported.

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools:
  - [V] **Models.** Claude-3, GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 via API; Gemma2 2B, IBM-Granite 3B and Qwen3 8B open-weight (p. 5).
    - Temperature is 1 for the API models and 0.4 for the open models, "as reported in prior work" (p. 5).
    - Exact API model versions: not reported.
  - [V] **Granite responses.** The BigCodeBench responses came from the leaderboard and were re-run for the constrained comparison (p. 10).
  - [V] **Hardware.** "a local computer with an M2 processor, 8-core CPU, 10-core GPU, and 24GB RAM" (p. 17).
  - [V] **Decoding.** llama.cpp's parser, with an added state cache for the parser's pushdown automata. llama.cpp samples first and applies the grammar mask only when the sample is rejected (p. 4).
  - [V] **Grammar construction.** Converting the Python grammar to GBNF took about 4 h by hand. Each library-grammar step takes under a second (pp. 4, 16).
  - [V] **Detection time.** Mypy about 1 s; Pyright and the grammar about 2.5 s; o3-mini about 4 s (p. 19).
  - [V] **Constrained-decoding cost.** Unconstrained responses average 22.3 s, constrained 34.76 s (p. 11).
- Code availability: not reported (no repository link found).

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] **Precision and recall on all errors.**
  - [V] **Imaginary Feature Recall (IFR):** recall on the examples containing Attribute, Import, Type or ModuleNotFound errors (p. 5).
  - [V] **RIF:** imaginary features as a share of the errors left after repair (p. 5).
  - [V] **Pass@1, Execution Rate (ER) and IF%.** IF% is the share of samples with one of the four error types (p. 5).
  - [V] **Manual-analysis measures:** Caught, TP (correctly identified for the right reason), Overlap, Capable (p. 7).
  - [I] RIF is a relative measure. It can rise when repair removes *other* errors while hallucinations stay the same, and fall when other errors remain. Changes in RIF are not changes in the absolute number of hallucinations.
- Statistical testing:
  - [V] Cohen's kappa for annotation agreement, average 0.79 (pp. 7, 18).
  - [V] Spearman correlation between the full and the validated benchmark: 0.98 for detection, 0.99 for constrained decoding, 0.88 for repair (p. 12).
  - No CIs, significance tests or multi-run variance.

## 7. Key findings
1. **Abstract figures.**
   - [A] LLMs use non-existent library features in "8.1-40% of responses" (p. 1).
   - [A] Static tools detect "16-70% of all errors, and 14-85% of library hallucinations" (p. 1).
   - [I] "14-85%" matches Pyright's IFR range in Table 10 (0.14–0.85, p. 20).
   - [I] "8.1-40%" and "16-70%" could not be matched to any table. Pyright's all-error recall is 0.16–0.82 (p. 6). The no-repair RIF is 8.1–44.9 (p. 10), but that is a share of errors, not of responses. Table 6 gives IF% of 4.4–22.2 for the open models (p. 11).
2. [V] **Detection recall on all errors** (Table 1, p. 6).
   - Pyright has the highest recall overall, e.g. 0.70 for claude-3 on DS-1000 and 0.82 for gpt-4 on Odex.
   - Grammar recall is 0.04–0.22.
   - o3-mini has high precision and low recall.
3. [V] **Detection recall on hallucinations (IFR)** (pp. 7, 20).
   - By method: Pyright 0.14–0.85; Mypy 0.03–0.70; grammar 0.06–0.20; o3-mini 0.02–0.78. o3-mini does better on the small models.
   - Automatic precision on hallucinations was 1, except one cell at 0.98.
   - [A] Mypy and the grammar do best on ImportError/ModuleNotFound; Pyright does better on Type/AttributeError (p. 6).
   - [V] **These are recall figures from automatic error matching.** In the manual sample, the share of hallucinations flagged for the right reason (TP) by the static tools is only 37.6% (DS-1000), 4.0% (Odex) and 10.0% (BigCode). The share flagged at all (Caught) is 56.7%, 19.0% and 23.0% (Table 2, p. 8).
4. [V] **Manual upper bound** (Table 2, p. 8).
   - Share of hallucinations each method could catch ("Capable"): static tools 77.0% (DS-1000), 70.5% (Odex), 48.5% (BigCode); grammar 18.0%, 10.5%, 7.0%.
   - [A] "after manual inspection we found that false positives mean the true upper bound is 77%" (p. 12).
5. [V] **Benchmark noise.**
   - Ambiguous input plus ambiguous output make up 36.9% of the sampled hallucinations in Odex, 34.1% in BigCode and 1.1% in DS-1000 (p. 9). In Table 3 these are input 6.6/7.5% plus output 30.3/26.6% (p. 8).
   - This supports the authors' "over 30%" claim for Odex and BigCode (p. 9).
   - Removing noisy items (3% / 7.7% / 6.1%) preserves model rankings (p. 12).
6. [V] **Repair raises execution rate and Pass@1** (Table 4, p. 9), e.g. Gemma2 2B on DS-1000: ER 47.2 → 77.9 with o3+Self.

   Its effect on the hallucination share (RIF, Table 5, p. 10) depends on the benchmark:
   - **DS-1000: RIF falls for every model and every repair method.** Examples: claude-3 9.1 → 2.7; Gemma2 2B 22.3 → 5.8–8.1; Qwen3 8B 25.4 → 6.1–13.4; Granite 3B 17.2 → 11.9–13.9.
   - **BigCode: roughly flat for the large models (within ±2 points); falls modestly in most small-model cells.** Gemma2 44.9 → 35.7–42.7; Granite 43.9 → 38.2–39.0; Qwen3 31.8 → 23.1 with Mypy, but 36.4 with Pyright.
   - **Odex: flat or slightly up for the large models; rises sharply for the small models.** claude-3 20.4 → 16.2–16.6; gpt-4 13.7 → 15.6–16.0; Gemma2 23.8 → 27.8–51.0; Granite 24.0 → 46.6–48.9; Qwen3 31.3 → 47.8–55.6.

   [A] The authors summarise this as "In most cases, there is no improvement in fixing hallucinations" (p. 10) and say the hallucination rate "remained unchanged across all benchmarks" (p. 12). Both overstate Table 5, which shows clear improvement on DS-1000. [I] Because RIF is relative (§6), none of these changes can be read as absolute reductions in hallucinations.
7. [V] **Constrained decoding** (Table 6, p. 11) changes IF% by small, mixed amounts:
   - Odex: Gemma 5.4 → 4.8; Granite 8.9 → 8.2; Qwen 6 → 4.4.
   - DS-1000: Granite 10.4 → 6.7, but Gemma 10.4 → 12.6.
   - Pass@1 sometimes drops.
   - It adds about 12 s per request.

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] Python only. Other languages need a hand-converted grammar and an adapted script (pp. 4, 12).
- [A] The grammar cannot handle atypical aliases, because llama.cpp grammars cannot track state (p. 16). It also cannot link attributes imported via `from ... import` (p. 8).
- [A] Docstrings are incomplete (e.g. namespaces, dtype). This causes grammar errors and lowers Pass@1 (pp. 8, 10).
- [A] Static tools miss data-flow and control-flow cases, such as lambda/map/apply and changing types (pp. 7–8).
- [A] After agreement was checked, a single annotator labelled the remaining two-thirds (p. 7).
- [A] Memoisation gave no speed gain; latency needs further analysis (p. 19).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Package existence is judged against the benchmark environment, not a registry.**
  - ModuleNotFoundError is defined as "does not exist in the environment and/or in real life" (p. 18), and the grammar validates imports against the benchmark environment (p. 4).
  - Real packages that are simply not installed are therefore merged with invented ones.
  - The paper says nothing about whether names exist on PyPI, or about squatting.
- [I] **Package-level results are a small, unseparated part.**
  - In the manual sample, the "Library" cause category (functions, parameters and constants defined in a library; Table 9, p. 19) is only 14.7% (DS-1000), 6.6% (Odex) and 6.0% (BigCode) (Table 3, p. 8).
  - Detection metrics are not broken down by cause, and ModuleNotFound (package-level) cases are not reported separately.
- [I] **Detection ranges overstate what the tools achieve.** IFR counts matched error types, but correct-for-the-right-reason detection by the static tools is 4.0–37.6% in the manual sample (p. 8).
- [I] **Authors' summary of repair is too negative.** As shown in §7 finding 6, the repair text (pp. 10, 12) contradicts Table 5 on DS-1000.
- [I] **Abstract ranges partly untraceable.** "8.1-40%" and "16-70%" could not be matched to any table; "14-85%" matches Pyright IFR (p. 20).
- [I] **Unspecified model versions and mixed temperatures.** API model versions are not given, and temperatures differ between closed (1.0) and open (0.4) models. This confounds model comparisons.
- [I] **Inconsistent annotation share.** The double-annotated share is "One third" on p. 7 but "25%" in the Table 8 caption (p. 18).
- [I] **Thin reproducibility and statistics.** No CIs, a single Pass@1 sample, and no reported code release.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal:
  - o3-mini is both a detector baseline and the repair model.
  - Granite outputs come from different sources across experiments (p. 10).
  - RIF is a relative metric, so its direction can reflect changes in other error types.
- External:
  - Python only, three benchmarks.
  - Older closed models (Claude-3, GPT-3.5/4) and small open models.
  - No agentic setting.
- Construct:
  - "Hallucination" is defined by runtime error types against an installed environment.
  - Benchmark underspecification inflates counts; the authors partly correct for this (pp. 9, 12).
  - Automatic detection credit exceeds correct-reason detection (p. 8).
- Statistical conclusion: no tests or CIs. Annotation agreement is substantial (kappa 0.79) (p. 7).
- Reproducibility: hardware and benchmarks are reported; model versions, code and outputs are not.

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A]:
  - use the model's internal states for detection (p. 12);
  - extend static tools with data-flow and control-flow tracking (pp. 7–8);
  - build benchmarks that accept multiple valid solutions and specify input/output types (p. 9);
  - study where hallucinations originate (p. 12);
  - extend to other languages (p. 4).
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - add a registry-existence layer (PyPI/npm) to the static pipeline, so "not installed", "does not exist" and "exists but is a squat" are kept apart;
  - report package-level (ModuleNotFound) results and absolute hallucination counts after repair separately.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids):
  - RQ3: static analysis and constrained decoding as cheap defences, with their cost and effectiveness.
  - RQ4: ground truth taken from the installed environment, benchmark-noise pitfalls, annotation reliability.
  - RQ1: hallucination shares across small and large models (partial).
  - RQ5: laptop feasibility.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Proof of laptop feasibility.** The whole study ran on an M2 machine with 24 GB RAM, including constrained decoding of 2–8B models (p. 17). It is the only laptop-class run in this batch.
  - **Cheap import-level screening, with a catch.**
    - Mypy and Pyright with type stubs take about 1–2.5 s per sample (p. 19), a cheap check before running the code.
    - Their automatic detection credit overstates correct-reason detection (p. 8).
    - They check the *installed environment*, not the registry, so they cannot tell a slopsquatted package (which installs fine) from a legitimate one. A registry-aware check is still needed.
  - **Repair after detection is benchmark-dependent.** It lowered the hallucination share on DS-1000 but not on Odex for small models (p. 10). A defence study should report absolute hallucination counts, not just RIF.
  - **Constrained decoding is not worth it here:** about +12 s per request for small, inconsistent gains (p. 11).
  - **Measurement lesson:** separate benchmark noise from model hallucination, and hand-validate a subset.
  - **Evidence strength: moderate–weak.** It is a preprint (TMLR acceptance unverified) with a sound manual analysis, but its relevance at the package level is indirect.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ3 | Static tools' recall on library hallucinations (IFR) is 0.03–0.85 by model/benchmark (Pyright 0.14–0.85); but in a manual sample, correct-for-the-right-reason detection is only 37.6% (DS-1000), 4.0% (Odex), 10.0% (BigCode) | 8, 20 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Manual analysis caps static detection of hallucinations at 48.5–77% | 8, 12 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | LLM repair raises execution rate; the hallucination share of remaining errors (RIF) falls on DS-1000 for all models (e.g. claude-3 9.1 → 2.7), is roughly flat for large models on BigCode, and rises on Odex for small models (Qwen3 8B 31.3 → 55.6); the authors' "no improvement in most cases" overstates this | 9, 10, 12 | V (table) / A (summary) | moderate |
| RQ3 | Grammar-constrained decoding gives small, mixed IF% changes at about +12 s per request | 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | Ambiguous input/output in the benchmark accounts for 36.9% (Odex) and 34.1% (BigCode) of sampled hallucinations, vs 1.1% for DS-1000 | 8, 9 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | ModuleNotFound "hallucinations" are judged against the installed environment, not a package registry; library-definition causes are only 6.0–14.7% of the sample | 4, 8, 18 | V | moderate |
| RQ5 | Full pipeline incl. constrained decoding of 2–8B models ran on an M2 laptop (24 GB RAM); detection takes 1–4 s per sample | 17, 19 | V | moderate |

## 14. Key quotes
> "While repair consistently improves executability, imaginary features prove resistant." (p. 10)

> "after manual inspection we found that false positives mean the true upper bound is 77%" (p. 12)

> "This module does not exist in the environment and/or in real life." (p. 18)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 24 PDF pages, including appendices B–D. Figures 1, 3 and 6–12 are charts; we relied on the tables (Table 10 mirrors Figure 1) and the text.
- Uncertainties:
  - TMLR acceptance is an author claim; the paper is kept at preprint tier per the orchestrator decision.
  - "RIG" is undefined (p. 5).
  - "8.1-40%" and "16-70%" in the abstract are untraced.
- Critical-review fixes (2026-11-12):
  - **Applied:**
    - RIF/repair claim corrected against Table 5 in the main finding, §6, §7.6, §9, §10, §12 and §13;
    - abstract range traceability (14–85% = Pyright IFR);
    - TP alongside recall;
    - Library-cause shares;
    - preprint tier.
  - **Partly applied:** the review's "≈27–30%" for benchmark underspecification counts only ambiguous *output*. Page 9 gives 36.9% (Odex) and 34.1% (BigCode) for ambiguous input plus output, consistent with Table 3 (p. 8). That supports the authors' "over 30%", so the RQ4 row is now [V] with those figures.

---
key: ohm2020backstabbers
status: complete
evidence_basis: full-text
design: Manually curated dataset of real malicious packages + qualitative attack-tree taxonomy (descriptive statistics)
dataset: 174 malicious packages from npm (109), PyPI (28), RubyGems (37) used in real attacks, Nov 2015-Nov 2019
sample_size: 174 packages analysed (of 469 identified; 59 proof-of-concept packages excluded)
metrics: descriptive shares (trigger phase, injection technique, conditional execution, objective, OS, obfuscation), Levenshtein distance, days to disclosure, code clusters
main_finding: Among 174 real malicious npm/PyPI/RubyGems packages, 61% used typosquatting and 56% executed at install time (PyPI: 75% and 96%).
relevance: medium
analysed: 2026-11-12
---

# Backstabber’s Knife Collection: A Review of Open Source Software Supply Chain Attacks

- Authors: Ohm, Marc; Plate, Henrik; Sykosch, Arnold; Meier, Michael
- Year / venue: 2020, Lecture Notes in Computer Science (book)
- DOI: 10.1007/978-3-030-52683-2_2 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-52683-2_2
- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index)

Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.

**Source tier:** Tier 2 (an LNCS proceedings chapter, per metadata), 2020.
- The analysed text is the arXiv v1 version (arXiv:2005.09535v1, 19 May 2020; p. 1). It may differ slightly from the published chapter.
- We use it as **background** because it predates LLMs, not because of its source quality. It is a seminal paper (241 citations per metadata).

## 1. Research objective
- [A] Give a structured overview of how attackers inject malicious code into open-source dependency trees and trigger it. The goal is to support preventive and detective safeguards (p. 1).
- [A] Provide a manually curated dataset of malicious packages used in real-world attacks (pp. 1–2).

## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
- No formal RQs. There are two contributions (p. 2):
  1. manual analysis and categorisation of 174 real malicious packages (2015–2019);
  2. two attack trees, one for *injection* and one for *execution*.

## 3. Methodology
- Research design: [V] Qualitative and descriptive (pp. 4–5).
  - The attack trees were built iteratively. Each malicious package or information source was mapped to a node; a new node was added when none fitted.
  - Packages were analysed and categorised by hand.
- Approach — the attack trees (read from Fig. 2, p. 7, and Fig. 3, p. 9):
  - [V] **Injection tree.** Root: "Injection of Malicious Code (into dependency tree)" (p. 7).
    - **Create New Package**: Trojan Horse; Typosquatting; Use After Free (p. 7).
    - **Infect Existing Package** (p. 7):
  - [V] **Execution tree** (p. 9). Root: "Execute Malicious Behavior".
    - During Different Life Cycle Phases: Install Scripts; Test Case; Runtime.
    - Conditional Execution: Application State; Dependency Tree; Operating System.
  - [A] **New packages.** A new package "using a name that is not used by anybody else avoids interference with other legitimate project maintainers. However, such a package has to be discovered and referenced by downstream users", for example via typosquatting or by promoting a trojan horse (p. 7).
  - [A] **Install-time execution.** "Such install scripts exist for Python and Node.js" and run automatically during installation (p. 8).
  - [A] **Import-time execution.** In Python, code can be triggered at runtime by putting it in `__init__.py`, which runs on `import` (p. 9).
- Baselines or comparison conditions: not applicable (descriptive study).

## 4. Dataset and sample
- Data source(s):
  - [V] The authors reviewed the Snyk vulnerability database, language-specific security advisories and research blogs between 2 July and 2 August 2019, and updated the review on 27 January 2020 (p. 4).
  - [V] The registries had removed the malicious code, so it was retrieved from deprecated mirrors, internet archives and research repositories (p. 4).
  - [V] Publication dates come from Libraries.io (p. 5).
- Sample size (N) and unit:
  - [V] 469 malicious packages were identified; 59 proof-of-concept packages were excluded; at least one malicious version was obtained for 174 (p. 9).
  - [V] Download success by registry (pp. 9–10):

    | Registry | Obtained / identified | Rate |
    |---|---|---|
    | npm | 109/374 | 29.14% |
    | PyPI | 28/44 | 63.64% |
    | RubyGems | 37/41 | 90.24% |
    | Maven Central | 0/10 | 0% |

  - [V] Composition of the 174: npm 62.6%, PyPI 16.1%, RubyGems 21.3% (p. 10).
- Sampling / selection method: [V] Every malicious package found in the sources whose code could be obtained (pp. 4, 9). This is a convenience sample of *disclosed* and *retrievable* attacks.
- Data availability: [V] On GitHub, but "access will be granted on justified request only due to ethical reasons" (p. 10).

## 5. Experimental setup
- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Manual code analysis (pp. 4–5, 11–16).
  - Confirms maliciousness.
  - Classifies each package by trigger, conditions, injection technique, objective, targeted OS and obfuscation.
  - Finds clusters through code reuse and dependency relations.
  - The number of coders and their agreement are not reported.
- Code availability: not applicable / not reported.

## 6. Evaluation metrics
- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
  - [V] Category shares per registry and overall (Figs. 6–11).
  - [V] Days between publication and disclosure.
  - [V] Levenshtein (edit) distance from a typosquat to its target.
  - [V] Cluster size and timing (pp. 10–16).
- Statistical testing: descriptive statistics only (mean, min, max, standard deviation, median; pp. 11–12, 15). No tests.

## 7. Key findings
1. [V] **Exposure time.** On average a malicious package was available for 209 days before public reporting (median 67, max 1,216). PyPI had the highest average (p. 11).
2. [V] **Install-time execution dominates.**
   - Overall: 56% of packages trigger at install time, 43% at runtime, 1% in tests (p. 11).
   - By registry (Fig. 6, p. 11):
   - [I] The remaining 4% for PyPI appears to be runtime, judging from the bar shading and consistency with the overall 43%.
3. [V] **Conditional execution** (p. 12).
   - 41% of packages check a condition (application state, dependency tree or OS) before running. This helps them evade analysis sandboxes.
   - PyPI and RubyGems packages mostly run unconditionally.
4. [V] **Typosquatting dominates injection** (p. 12).
   - 61% of packages mimic existing names.
   - The mean edit distance to the target is 2.3 (median 1, max 11; e.g. `pythonkafka` → `kafka-python`).
   - Common techniques: adding or removing hyphens, dropping letters, swapping commonly mistyped letters.
   - [V] Some typosquats have distance 0: they reuse the exact name of a package from another repository, e.g. `python-sqlite`, which exists under the same name in the Linux apt repository (p. 12).
   - From Fig. 8: PyPI is 75% typosquatting and 25% trojan horse; overall, trojan horses are 11% (p. 13).
   - [V] A trojan horse is "a new package which consist of nothing but the malicious package", with "No meaningful typo-squatting targets" (p. 13).
5. [V] **Objectives.** Data exfiltration is the most common goal, at 55% of packages (pp. 16, 18).
   - Targets include `~/.ssh/*`, `~/.npmrc` and environment variables (p. 13).
   - 34% are droppers, 5% backdoors, 3% denial-of-service, 3% financial gain (p. 13).
   - 53% are OS-agnostic (p. 14). 49% use obfuscation, mostly Base64/hex encoding (pp. 14–15).
6. [V] **Clusters** (pp. 15–16).
   - 21 clusters cover 157 of the 174 packages (90%).
   - The largest (crossenv) has 36 packages, published in two waves.
   - One cluster spans npm and RubyGems.
7. [A] **Countermeasures.** These include multi-factor authentication for maintainers, "version pinning and disablement of install scripts for open source users", and isolated builds. They should be "enforced by default" (p. 16).

## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
- [A] The dataset is biased toward npm. No malicious packages could be obtained for Java (Maven) or PHP (p. 18).
- [A] About 34% are droppers whose second-stage payload may no longer be available (p. 18).
- [A] Most packages were downloaded from mirrors or archives, which is itself an injection vector in the tree. The authors argue the packages are still valid because maliciousness was confirmed by hand (p. 18).
- [A] The attack trees are not complete: they omit vectors not yet observed or described (p. 4).
- [A] How attackers select which package to infect cannot yet be validated from the data (p. 7).

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **Small PyPI sample.** Only 28 PyPI packages; the PyPI percentages rest on very few cases.
- [I] **Detected attacks only.** Only disclosed and retrievable attacks are included. Undetected or quickly deleted packages are missing, so the shares describe *detected* attacks.
- [I] **Unknown reliability of the hand coding.** Categorisation was done manually in a single pass, with no reported agreement between coders.
- [I] **Pre-LLM.** The attack tree has no node for discovery through automated recommendation, which is exactly the channel slopsquatting uses. Registry defences may have changed since 2019; the paper does not cover this.
- [I] **Bar-chart readings.** Per-registry shares are read from bar charts (Figs. 6–11), whose text extraction is garbled. We checked Figs. 6 and 8 against the PDF images.

## 10. Threats to validity
- Internal: the classification is subjective and manual, with no agreement measure.
- External: mostly npm; 2015–2019 only; registries and attacker tactics have changed since.
- Construct: "typosquatting" rests on a judgement of name similarity, and "trojan horse" is a catch-all category.
- Statistical conclusion: descriptive only; the PyPI subset is small.
- Reproducibility: the dataset is available on request (p. 10), and the attack trees are fully shown (pp. 7, 9).

## 11. Future research directions
- Stated by authors [A] (p. 18):
  - collect existing safeguards and run a gap analysis against the attack vectors;
  - scan whole repositories, exploiting code reuse across campaigns;
  - use the labelled dataset for supervised learning;
  - use the dataset as a benchmark, and keep curating it.
- Suggested by us [I]:
  - extend the injection tree with an "AI-recommended name" discovery node (slopsquatting) under Create New Package;
  - measure whether slopsquatted packages follow the same install-time and conditional-execution patterns.

## 12. Relevance to our research
- Research questions addressed (RQ ids):
  - RQ2: the attack model, i.e. how a registered name becomes malicious code running on the victim's machine.
  - RQ3: baseline countermeasures (disabling install scripts, version pinning).
  - RQ5: background for designing a safe study.
- How it informs our work [I]:
  - **Placing slopsquatting in the tree.**
    - It is a *Create New Package* attack, closest to the "trojan horse": a fresh name with no lookalike target.
    - It differs from typosquatting in how victims find the package. Here the LLM supplies the "discovery and referencing" step that the authors identify as the obstacle for new packages (p. 7).
  - **Pre-LLM analogue of name confusion.** [V] Some typosquats have edit distance 0 because they reuse an existing name from another repository (`python-sqlite` from apt; p. 12). This is a pre-LLM analogue of the cross-ecosystem and import-name confusion seen in raj2026names and twist2026library: a correct-looking name that resolves to someone else's package.
  - **Installing is enough to be compromised.**
    - Install-time execution is the main trigger on PyPI (96%; p. 11), and code can also run on import via `__init__.py` (p. 9).
    - An agent or user that runs `pip install` / `npm install` on a hallucinated name can be compromised immediately, so a defence must act **before** installation.
  - **Implication for a measurement study.**
    - Use read-only registry metadata; do not install packages.
    - Any dynamic analysis must run in a sandbox, since 41% of malicious packages run only under certain conditions (p. 12) and may evade sandboxes.
  - **Implication for a lightweight defence.**
    - Combine a pre-install existence/metadata check with the authors' user-side countermeasures: version pinning and disabled install scripts (p. 16).
    - The edit-distance profile of typosquats (mean 2.3, median 1; p. 12) can inform a lookalike check for hallucinated names.
  - **Evidence strength: moderate** as background. The data are real-world, but the study is descriptive, pre-2020, and the PyPI subset is small.

## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RQ2 | Attack tree: new malicious packages enter via Create New Package (trojan horse, typosquatting, use-after-free) but must be "discovered and referenced" by downstream users | 7 | A | moderate |
| RQ2 | 56% of 174 real malicious packages execute at install time (PyPI 96%, npm 64%); Python and Node.js support install scripts, and Python `__init__.py` runs on import | 8, 9, 11 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | 61% of malicious packages used typosquatting (PyPI 75%); mean edit distance to target 2.3, median 1; some reuse another repository's exact name (distance 0, e.g. python-sqlite from apt) | 12, 13 | V | moderate |
| RQ2 | Trojan-horse packages with no lookalike target are 11% overall and 25% on PyPI, the closest pre-LLM analogue to slopsquatted names | 13 | V (shares) / I (analogy) | weak |
| RQ2 | Malicious packages stayed available for 209 days on average (median 67) before disclosure; data exfiltration is the most common goal (55%) | 11, 18 | V | moderate |
| RQ4 | 41% of malicious packages execute only under conditions (app state, dependency tree, OS), which hinders sandbox-based dynamic detection | 12 | V | moderate |
| RQ3 | Recommended user-side countermeasures: version pinning and disabling install scripts, enforced by default | 16 | A | weak |

## 14. Key quotes
> "such a package has to be discovered and referenced by downstream users in order to end up in the dependency trees of victim packages" (p. 7)

> "Such install scripts exist for Python and Node.js, and may be used to perform pre- or post-installation activities." (p. 8)

> "most malicious packages (56%) start their routines on installation" (p. 11)

## Analyst notes
- Reading coverage: all 21 PDF pages.
  - Figs. 2, 3, 6 and 8 were read from the PDF images, because the extracted text of the trees and bar charts is garbled.
  - Figs. 7, 9, 10 and 11 were used only where the body text states the overall figure.
- Uncertainties:
  - The PyPI 4% segment in Fig. 6 (runtime vs test) is inferred from shading and arithmetic.
  - The published LNCS version was not compared with the arXiv text.
  - The conference behind the LNCS volume is not stated in the metadata or the text, so we do not name it.
- Critical-review fixes applied (2026-11-12):
  - tier wording;
  - data exfiltration at 55% (pp. 16, 18);
  - `python-sqlite` distance-0 typosquat (§7.4, §12, §13).
