1:# Evidence matrix — Package Hallucination and Slopsquatting in LLM Coding Assistants: Measuring Hallucinated Dependencies, Their Exploitability on PyPI/npm, and Lightweight Defences
182:## Contradictions
193:## Agreements / converging evidence
## Contradictions
<!-- Findings that disagree: which papers, what differs (data, method, population, metric), likely explanation (INTERPRETATION). -->

1. **Language direction (RQ1).** JavaScript > Python in [@spracklen2024we, p. 7] (per-test means 21.3% vs 15.8%); Python > JavaScript in [@krishna2025importing, p. 8] (23.14% vs 14.73%, per prompt) and for every model in [@churilov2026range, p. 7] (per mention). Differences: extraction (Spracklen asks the model for package lists and parses install commands and rejects import parsing, [@spracklen2024we, p. 6]; Krishna and Churilov parse imports, [@krishna2025importing, p. 12]; [@churilov2026range, p. 5]), unit (mention vs prompt), model cohort (2023–24 vs 2025–26). [I] Import parsing over-counts Python module names that differ from distribution names (cv2, sklearn), which plausibly explains much of the reversal.
2. **Prompt source on the same corpus (RQ1/RQ4).** Stack Overflow prompts > LLM-generated prompts for almost every model in [@spracklen2024we, p. 20]; LLM-generated > Stack Overflow for every model in [@churilov2026range, p. 7]. Same released prompt corpus, different models, extraction and time (2024 vs 2026). [I] Cleanest contradiction in the set; cause unresolved.
3. **Model size (RQ1).** Larger models hallucinate less in [@krishna2025importing, p. 6] (r = −0.542, but 33 pseudo-replicated points and an estimated 200B GPT-4o size, [@krishna2025importing, p. 3]); no size effect for Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 6]; newer Llama-3.1-8B produced more unique hallucinated names than Llama-3-8B in [@zhao2025hfuzzer, p. 7]. [I] Size is confounded with quantization (GPTQ for all open models in [@spracklen2024we, p. 6]; 4-bit ≤32B in [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10]; explicit quantization effects in [@haque2025secure, p. 6]).
4. **Temperature (RQ1).** Rates rise sharply above temperature 1 in [@spracklen2024we, p. 8]; no effect from 0 to 2 for Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 6]. Different ecosystem and extraction; not resolved.
5. **Import names: valid or hallucinated? (RQ4).** [@twist2026library, p. 4] counts any import name registered on PyPI as valid (PyPA normalisation only, [@twist2026library, p. 15]); [@raj2026names, p. 8] flags registered import names such as pil and faiss as squats; [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6] validates code-generation imports against the registry, so unregistered import names (cv2) probably count as hallucinations. [I] Method-driven contradiction: the field has no shared import→distribution mapping.
6. **RAG effect size (RQ3).** Large reductions in Python in [@spracklen2024we, p. 13] (CodeLlama 26.28% → 13.40%); negligible in Rust in [@zheng2026when, p. 8]; RAG slightly raises hallucination in [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 13] and raises JavaScript PHR in [@djire2026evaluating, p. 6]. [I] RAG is ecosystem- and retriever-dependent and not a reliable defence on its own.
7. **Real-world registration (RQ2) — compatible, not contradictory.** 25 of 2,282 hallucinated names registered within about six months, one with malware [@churilov2026range, p. 12]; 0 of 1,641 private names registered after 4 days and 22 of 149 public names registered, none malicious, 19 defensive placeholders [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 5]. Different windows and sampling frames.

## Agreements / converging evidence

- Every study that measures it finds non-zero package hallucination in all tested models, from 2023–24 open models ([@spracklen2024we, p. 7]) to 2026 frontier models ([@churilov2026range, p. 6]), and in Rust and Go as well as Python/JS ([@zheng2026when, p. 5]; [@haque2025secure, p. 6]).
- Hallucinated names are mostly model-specific with a persistent shared core: 81% single-model names in [@spracklen2024we, p. 10]; 104 names shared by all five 2026 models in [@churilov2026range, p. 9]; 450 of 455 new names single-model in [@okwor2026hallucination, p. 4]. Many recur across re-runs (43% in 10/10 runs, [@spracklen2024we, p. 9]).
- Registry existence checks are necessary but not sufficient: registered lookalikes and import-name collisions pass a plain 200/404 check ([@raj2026names, p. 8]; [@liu2026packmonitor, p. 6]; [@spracklen2024we, p. 12]).
- White-box defences (logit masking, model editing, unlearning) reach large reductions but need weights or logits and GPU servers ([@liu2026packmonitor, p. 12]; [@liu2026mitigating, p. 6]; [@spracklen2026llm, p. 8]); only static analysis ran on a laptop-class machine ([@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 17]).
- Models largely accept user-supplied fake package names (compliance, not invention): [@djire2026evaluating, p. 9]; [@twist2026library, p. 6]; [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].

## Design2Code: Benchmarking Multimodal Code Generation for Automated Front-End Engineering
> **Takeaway:** AI models can turn a screenshot of a webpage into code that looks quite similar, and GPT-4o was best on every visual measure [@si2025benchmarking, p. 6]. But the benchmark only checks how the page looks. It never checks whether anything works or whether the code is maintainable [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3].

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Chenglei Si, Yanzhe Zhang, Ryan Li, Zhengyuan Yang, Ruibo Liu, Diyi Yang |
| Year · Venue | 2025 · Proceedings of NAACL 2025 (Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1: Long Papers) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (conference long paper) |
| Identifier | DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.naacl-long.199 (arXiv 2403.03163) |
| Paper type | Benchmark with automatic metrics and a human evaluation |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (RQ3 only by absence) |

### In plain words
Front-end developers often turn a visual design into web code by hand. This paper asks how well AI models that read images (multimodal models) can do this automatically: you give them a screenshot of a real webpage, and they write the HTML and CSS [@si2025benchmarking, p. 1]. The authors built the first real-world test set for this task and new ways to score how close the result looks to the original. This is the starting point of the "screenshot to code" research line. It matters for us because many later reconstruction studies reuse its metrics, and because it clearly shows what visual scoring leaves out.

### How they did it
1. They took real webpages linked from C4 (a large public collection of web text), cleaned them and put all styling into one HTML file per page [@si2025benchmarking, p. 2].
2. Automatic filters cut the pool to 14k pages. Scripts, iframes, SVGs and external links were removed, and images were replaced by placeholders. The first two authors then hand-picked 484 test pages [@si2025benchmarking, p. 13].
3. Models were asked to write one HTML+CSS file from the screenshot. The prompt says no JavaScript is needed [@si2025benchmarking, p. 14].
4. They tried three prompting styles [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4]. Direct gives just the screenshot. Text-Augmented adds the page's text. Self-Revision lets the model see its own output and fix it.
5. They also fine-tuned (further trained on example data) their own open model, Design2Code-18B [@si2025benchmarking, p. 5].
6. They rendered each result and compared it with the original screenshot using five measures: Block-Match (are the text blocks there), Text, Position, Color and CLIP (overall visual similarity from an image-understanding model) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 4].
7. Paid human raters compared outputs in pairs and judged whether a generated page could replace the original [@si2025benchmarking, p. 5].

### Data and setup
- 484 test webpages, plus a harder set of 80 pages from GitHub [@si2025benchmarking, p. 8].
- Pages are long: 31,216 tokens and 158 HTML tags on average [@si2025benchmarking, p. 3].
- Models: GPT-4o, GPT-4V, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.0 Pro Vision, several open models and two fine-tuned models [@si2025benchmarking, p. 5].
- Commercial models used greedy decoding (always the most likely output), so one run per setting [@si2025benchmarking, p. 14].
- Human evaluation: 100 sampled pages, 5 raters per item, 60 participants in total [@si2025benchmarking, p. 15].

### Key findings
- [V] GPT-4o Direct is best on all automatic measures: Block 93.0, Text 98.2, Position 85.5, Color 84.1, CLIP 90.4 [@si2025benchmarking, p. 6]. Humans preferred it over the Gemini baseline 92% of the time [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- [A] Models "mostly lag in recalling visual elements" and in getting the layout right [@si2025benchmarking, p. 1].
- [V] On the hard set, Block-Match falls to 56.6 to 75.1, and GPT-4o Direct scores 56.6 [@si2025benchmarking, p. 8].
- [V] Adding the page text raised Block-Match for 4 of 7 models but lowered it for GPT-4o (93.0 to 92.4) and Claude 3 Opus (90.2 to 89.8) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 6].
- [V] 49% of GPT-4V self-revised pages were judged able to replace the original [@si2025benchmarking, p. 6].
- [V] The measures predict human preference with 79.9% accuracy. Exact text similarity counted negatively: humans care more about layout and content than exact wording [@si2025benchmarking, p. 7].
- [V] Human raters agreed only moderately or weakly with each other: Fleiss' kappa (a chance-corrected agreement score) of 0.46, 0.32 and 0.26 [@si2025benchmarking, p. 16].
- [V] Pages with more HTML tags are harder (r = −0.28 with Block-Match) [@si2025benchmarking, p. 15].

## When LLMs Invent Rust Crates: An Empirical Study of Hallucination Patterns and Mitigation
> **Takeaway:** In Rust code written by six AI models, about one in five references to a crate (a Rust package) pointed to a crate that does not exist, and model size and temperature barely changed this [@zheng2026when, p. 5; @zheng2026when, p. 6]. Almost half of these "invented crates" are mix-ups with Rust's own standard library, and part of the count may come from the authors' name parser, so treat the headline rate with care.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Jieming Zheng, Hao Guan, Yepang Liu |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed); a reported conference acceptance is not verified |
| Identifier | arXiv 2606.08444 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2606.08444) |
| Paper type | Measurement study plus a prompt-based mitigation experiment |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
Rust is a programming language. Its packages are called "crates" and are published on the registry crates.io. A package hallucination happens when an AI model names a package that does not exist. This is a security risk, because an attacker can register the invented name and fill it with malware. That attack is called slopsquatting. Earlier studies looked at Python and JavaScript; the authors present this as the first large study for Rust [@zheng2026when, p. 1]. One caveat matters for us: in Rust, mentioning a crate in a source file does not download it [@zheng2026when, p. 1]. So this paper measures names in generated text, not what actually gets installed.

### How they did it
1. They built 2,794 Rust coding tasks from three sources: 1,001 Stack Overflow questions, 793 tasks made from documented functions in popular GitHub projects, and 1,000 tasks that a Qwen model wrote from crate descriptions [@zheng2026when, p. 2; @zheng2026when, p. 3].
2. Each model wrote code for every task with its default settings [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
3. A script pulled crate names out of the code with three text patterns: use lines, path prefixes such as name::item, and extern crate lines [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
4. Each name was compared with a reference list: every crates.io name, plus Rust's standard and compiler crates and known aliases. Any name not on the list counted as hallucinated [@zheng2026when, p. 4; @zheng2026when, p. 5].
5. The main measure is the Crate Hallucination Rate (CHR): hallucinated references divided by all extracted references [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
6. To describe patterns they used edit distance (how many single-letter changes turn one name into another) and the overlap of invented names between models [@zheng2026when, p. 7].
7. They tested two prompt-based fixes on the three open models. Self-refinement asks the model to check its own crate names and regenerate up to 3 times. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) adds descriptions of 5 matching crates, drawn from the 10,000 most-downloaded, to the prompt [@zheng2026when, p. 8].

### Data and setup
- 14 model variants from six families: GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Opus, Qwen2.5-Coder (0.5B to 32B), DeepSeek-Coder-V2 (16B and 236B) and OpenCoder (1.5B and 8B). "B" means billions of parameters, a rough measure of model size [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
- Main run: 16,764 code snippets with 48,494 extracted crate references [@zheng2026when, p. 5]. [I] That is one answer per task per model.
- Temperature (a setting that makes output more random) was varied from 0 to 2 on four models [@zheng2026when, p. 6].
- Open models were run through Ollama, a tool for running models locally, on a server with 8 RTX 6000 Ada GPUs [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
- Not reported: the quantization level of the Ollama models and the date of the crates.io name list.
- Tasks, prompts, scripts and results are shared on figshare [@zheng2026when, p. 10].

### Key findings
- [V] 10,779 of 48,494 crate references were hallucinated, an overall CHR of 22.23% [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
- [V] Gemini 2.5 Pro had the lowest rate (16.18%) and Claude 4 Opus the highest (26.90%) [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
- [V] Size did not predict the rate within Qwen2.5-Coder (p = 0.912). Temperature had no significant effect (p = 0.4859), while the choice of model did (p = 0.0173) [@zheng2026when, p. 5; @zheng2026when, p. 6].
- [V] 45.47% of hallucinations are standard-library or internal modules treated as outside crates, led by thread and duration [@zheng2026when, p. 6].
- [V] The other invented names sit close to real ones: 40.78% are 1–2 edits from a real crate and 86.48% within 5; 32.96% drop a hyphen that the real crate has [@zheng2026when, p. 7].
- [V] 38.9% of frequently invented names are borrowed from other ecosystems, such as queryparser from Python [@zheng2026when, p. 8].
- [V] Self-refinement lowered the rate by 2.22–3.26 points. RAG lowered it by 1.92 and 0.96 points for two models and raised it by 0.34 for Qwen2.5-Coder [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
- [A] The authors conclude that prompt-level methods alone are insufficient [@zheng2026when, p. 9].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Whether invented crates would be installed, break builds or be exploitable was not measured [@zheng2026when, p. 10].
- [A] Alias coverage is incomplete, so the true rate is "likely slightly lower" [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
- [A] One third of the tasks were written by a Qwen model, and models change quickly [@zheng2026when, p. 10].
- [I] The path-prefix pattern may also catch type names such as Duration::from_secs. Odd top-10 names such as trefcell and tu32 look like a parser bug that the paper does not discuss [@zheng2026when, p. 6].
- [I] The counts do not match: 10,779 hallucinated references in one section, 13,332 non-module occurrences in the next [@zheng2026when, p. 5; @zheng2026when, p. 7].
- [I] The abstract claims "surprisingly consistent" rates and no loss of code quality, but the model effect is significant and code quality was never measured [@zheng2026when, p. 1; @zheng2026when, p. 6].
- [I] The paper does not say how hyphens in crate names were matched to underscores in code, which affects the 32.96% hyphen finding.
- [I] Ollama's default downloads are usually quantized, so size comparisons may be mixed up with precision. One answer per task, no confidence intervals, preprint.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] G1: installation through Cargo, Rust's package tool, was not measured [@zheng2026when, p. 10]. What models actually install remains open.
- [A] G2: the authors propose a Rust-aware guard that separates standard modules from outside crates, checks near-miss names against the registry and cross-checks the project's Cargo.toml file, but they do not test it [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
- [I] G3: its unit (every source-level reference, including standard-library mix-ups) differs from other papers' units, so 22% cannot be compared directly with Python or JavaScript rates [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
- [I] G4: the unreported quantization of the Ollama models is one more hidden confound.
- [A] The prompt fixes still need testing on commercial models [@zheng2026when, p. 9].

### Why it matters for your research
This is the only Rust study in the set, and it is large. Its main lesson is about measurement: the reference list and the parser decide much of the rate, so any study of yours should hand-check a sample of flagged names. The near-miss pattern (most invented names are a few letters from a real one) supports adding a lookalike check to a pre-install guard. The small Qwen2.5-Coder models it used run on a laptop through Ollama, and its data are public, so a partial replication is cheap.

### Connections to other papers
- [V] Temperature: spracklen2024we found rates rising sharply above temperature 1 [@spracklen2024we, p. 8]; here there was no effect for Rust (evidence matrix contradiction 4).
- [V] Size: krishna2025importing found that larger models hallucinate less [@krishna2025importing, p. 6]; no size effect here (contradiction 3).
- [V] RAG cut Python rates sharply in spracklen2024we [@spracklen2024we, p. 13] but helped little here (contradiction 6).
- [I] spracklen2024we reported that 48.6% of invented Python names are 6 or more edits from a real one [@spracklen2024we, p. 11]. This paper counts occurrences rather than names, so the two figures are not directly comparable.
- [V] When the fake name is planted in the prompt, dasu2026refusing finds nonexistent Rust crates fabricated on 87% of prompts [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8]. That measures accepting a name, not inventing one.

{"hookSpecificOutput":{"hookEventName":"SubagentStart","additionalContext":"PONYTAIL MODE ACTIVE — level: full

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications that cut a real corner with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic) with a `ponytail:` comment naming the ceiling and upgrade path (`# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`).

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.

## Refusing the Impossible: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Code Hallucination in Large Language Models
> **Takeaway:** When a coding request names a package that does not exist, open AI models usually write code for it instead of saying it does not exist, and bigger models barely do better on this [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6; @dasu2026refusing, p. 8]. The fake name is written into the prompt, so this paper measures how often models accept a planted name, not how often they invent one.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Vishnu Asutosh Dasu, Ashish Kundu, Gang Tan |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed) |
| Identifier | arXiv 2609.03267 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2609.03267) |
| Paper type | Benchmark and evaluation study with an AI judge checked against human labels |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |

### In plain words
Most coding benchmarks contain only tasks that can be solved. This paper asks what happens when a request cannot be satisfied, for example because it names a package that does not exist or asks for an impossible algorithm. The right answer is to refuse [@dasu2026refusing, p. 1]. The authors call code built on something that does not exist "code hallucination", sort these failures into a taxonomy (a structured list of types), and release a benchmark to test them [@dasu2026refusing, p. 1]. Matched solvable tasks check that a model is not simply refusing everything.

### How they did it
1. They hand-wrote 270 unsatisfiable requests in 24 subcategories. One family covers plausible but nonexistent things, such as packages on PyPI, npm, crates.io and Go, Java APIs and C headers [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
2. Each request comes with a note naming the planted fake item, for example a crate called serde_ultra [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
3. They added 91 solvable control tasks that differ only slightly from the fake ones [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
4. Requests cover six programming languages and ten "framings", such as internal documentation or a learner's question [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
5. 17 open-weight models (models whose weights can be downloaded) each answered once at temperature 0, the least random setting [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
6. Claude Opus 4.6 acted as judge with a fixed rubric, labelling each answer as correct, hallucination or refusal [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
7. The judge was checked against 138 human labels, and results carry 95% bootstrap intervals (ranges of likely values found by resampling the prompts) [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].

### Data and setup
- 6,137 judged responses from 17 models with 6.7B to 671B parameters [@dasu2026refusing, p. 1].
- Models up to 32B ran with 4-bit quantization (weights stored with fewer bits to save memory); larger ones ran at full precision [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
- The package subsets are small: twelve nonexistent npm prompts and ten nonexistent crate prompts [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9].
- Judge agreement with humans: 94% on outcomes, Cohen's kappa 0.91 (an agreement score corrected for chance, where 1 is perfect) [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
- Inference software and hardware are not reported. Code and prompts are released [@dasu2026refusing, p. 2].

### Key findings
- [V] Models wrote ungrounded code for 54% of unsatisfiable requests and refused 31% [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5]. Only 1 of 1,547 control answers was a wrongful refusal [@dasu2026refusing, p. 2].
- [V] Scale helps with impossible tasks (hallucination 0.84 for small models, 0.32 for the largest) but much less with nonexistent things (0.88 to 0.61), and least with fake npm packages and Rust crates (1.00 to 0.85) [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6].
- [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B) and gpt-oss 120B fabricated code for every nonexistent npm and crate prompt [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6].
- [V] By ecosystem, nonexistent npm packages were fabricated on 94% of prompts, Rust crates 87%, Go modules and PyPI modules 63% each, and Java APIs 33% [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
- [V] A misspelled real package name led to fabrication on only 14% of prompts, against 94% for a correctly spelled fake one [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
- [V] 66% of hallucinations were confident fabrications without any caveat [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6].
- [V] Wording matters more than the model: prompt identity explains 34% of outcome variation against 15% for model identity [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
- [V] One model suggested pip install pywfm, a name that already exists on PyPI as an unrelated 2015 package [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Template prompts may differ from what developers type, so absolute rates belong to this benchmark [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
- [A] One answer per prompt; the judge sees the note on the fake item, and the human gold set was labelled by one author [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
- [A] Model size is confounded with 4-bit quantization, and closed models were not tested [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
- [I] The user supplies the fake name, so rates such as 94% are not comparable with spontaneous invention rates from other studies.
- [I] Package results rest on 22 prompts per model, so per-model package rates are uncertain.
- [I] The judge agreed with humans on only 67% of behaviour labels, so behaviour shares are indicative [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
- [I] Publishing the fake names lets anyone register them, which could change the ground truth for future replications.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [A] G1: closed frontier models and agentic settings are not evaluated [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
- [A] G2: the authors recommend checking package names against registries at generation time but do not test it [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9].
- [A] G4: size is confounded with quantization [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10]. The gap report lists this as a hidden confound across studies.
- [I] Typo amplification was dropped as a gap in our gap report because this paper and twist2026library already measure it [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].

### Why it matters for your research
This is the clearest evidence that larger models do not fix fake-package acceptance. Its benchmark is small and public, and its small models already ran at 4-bit, the setting a laptop uses. A laptop study could re-run the npm, crate and PyPI subsets on local 7B models and test whether a simple registry check before installing reduces harm. Two design habits are worth copying: matched solvable controls and an AI judge validated against human labels.

### Connections to other papers
- [V] twist2026library finds the same acceptance of fake names, up to 99.22% of tasks [@twist2026library, p. 6], as does djire2026evaluating [@djire2026evaluating, p. 9].
- [V] twist2026library reports one-character typos accepted in up to 25.86% of tasks [@twist2026library, p. 6]. Here a typo that the model corrects counts as correct, which may explain the lower 14% [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
- [I] On model size, krishna2025importing finds a size effect [@krishna2025importing, p. 6] and zheng2026when none [@zheng2026when, p. 5]. The quantization confound here shows why size results disagree (evidence matrix contradiction 3).
- [V] The pywfm case is a real-world example of what spracklen2024we warns: a plain existence check passes names that are already registered [@spracklen2024we, p. 12].
EOF

> **Takeaway:** When a coding request names a package that does not exist, open AI models usually write code for it instead of saying it does not exist, and bigger models barely do better on this [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6; @dasu2026refusing, p. 8]. The fake name is written into the prompt, so this paper measures how often models accept a planted name, not how often they invent one.

| Item | Detail |

| Authors | Vishnu Asutosh Dasu, Ashish Kundu, Gang Tan |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed) |
| Identifier | arXiv 2609.03267 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2609.03267) |
| Paper type | Benchmark and evaluation study with an AI judge checked against human labels |
| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |

Matched solvable tasks check that a model is not simply refusing everything.

1. They hand-wrote 270 unsatisfiable requests in 24 subcategories. One family covers plausible but nonexistent things, such as packages on PyPI, npm, crates.io and Go, Java APIs and C headers [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].

## LLM Hallucinations in Practical Code Generation: Phenomena, Mechanism, and Mitigation
> **Takeaway:** In realistic Python tasks set inside real projects, most AI coding mistakes come from misunderstanding the task, and problems with missing packages make up under 1% of hallucinations [@zhang2025llm, p. 4; @zhang2025llm, p. 6]. Read it as background: it maps the kinds of code hallucination, but it does not measure invented PyPI packages.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Ziyao Zhang, Chong Wang, Yanlin Wang, Ensheng Shi, Yuchi Ma, Wanjun Zhong, Jiachi Chen, Mingzhi Mao, Zibin Zheng (published version; our arXiv copy lists five authors) |
| Year · Venue | 2025 · Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), ISSTA 2025 issue |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (PACMSE / ISSTA 2025); our copy is the arXiv version |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1145/3728894 (arXiv 2409.20550) |
| Paper type | Empirical study: hand-built taxonomy of errors plus a small mitigation pilot |
| Relevance to us | Low — RQ1 (marginal), RQ3 and RQ4 (background) |

### In plain words
Many studies test AI coding on small, self-contained functions. This paper uses repository-level tasks instead: the model must write a function that fits into a real project with its own files and dependencies [@zhang2025llm, p. 1]. The authors read thousands of generated snippets and sorted the mistakes into a taxonomy (a structured list of error types) [@zhang2025llm, p. 3; @zhang2025llm, p. 4]. Package hallucination is only one small corner of that map. The paper is useful to us mainly for context and for a warning about definitions.

### How they did it
1. They used CoderEval Python, a benchmark of 230 tasks taken from real projects, each with tests and a working project environment [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
2. Six models produced 10 answers per task with nucleus sampling at temperature 0.6, a moderately random setting [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
3. Two authors open-coded (read examples and created labels from what they saw) 1,380 snippets from 23 tasks to build the first version of the taxonomy [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
4. Three volunteers labelled the remaining snippets, and one author reviewed all labels [@zhang2025llm, p. 3; @zhang2025llm, p. 10].
5. They compared models and proposed root causes [@zhang2025llm, p. 8].
6. A pilot fix used RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): it added the 10 most similar code snippets from the same project to the prompt. Success was measured by Pass@1, the share of tasks where the first answer passes the tests [@zhang2025llm, p. 9].

### Data and setup
- Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo, CodeGen-350M, PanGu-alpha-2.6B, DeepSeekCoder-6.7B, CodeLlama-7B-Python and StarCoder2-7B [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
- [I] 230 tasks × 6 models × 10 answers gives 13,800 snippets by our arithmetic; the paper does not state the total number of hallucinations.
- A "non-existent package" means one that is not available in the task's environment [@zhang2025llm, p. 6]. There is no check against PyPI.
- Code, data and results are on GitHub [@zhang2025llm, p. 1]. Hardware and exact prompts are not reported.

### Key findings
- [V] Three categories: task requirement conflicts 43.53%, factual knowledge conflicts 31.91% and project context conflicts 24.56% of hallucinations [@zhang2025llm, p. 4; @zhang2025llm, p. 5; @zhang2025llm, p. 6].
- [V] Environment conflicts, which include importing a package missing from the environment, are only 0.94%. The example is a package called _lfu_cache [@zhang2025llm, p. 6].
- [I] _lfu_cache is not a valid PyPI distribution name, so it is probably a missing internal module. The 0.94% is therefore an upper bound on invented-package cases.
- [V] API knowledge conflicts are much more common (20.41%), for example a parameter that a real function does not have, as in timedelta(year=1) [@zhang2025llm, p. 6].
- [V] Library knowledge conflicts make up 2.68% [@zhang2025llm, p. 5].
- [V] One security-relevant example: generated code used yaml.load instead of the safer safe_load [@zhang2025llm, p. 5].
- [V] Task requirement conflicts are the most frequent category for all six models [@zhang2025llm, p. 8].
- [V] RAG raised Pass@1 for every model, for example ChatGPT from 10.40% to 12.61% and CodeLlama from 2.17% to 5.22%. [A] The authors call the gain modest [@zhang2025llm, p. 9].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] Python only and only 230 tasks [@zhang2025llm, p. 10].
- [A] No formal inter-rater reliability measure (a statistic for how far independent labellers agree) [@zhang2025llm, p. 10].
- [I] The fix was judged by Pass@1, not by counting hallucinations, so it does not show that RAG reduces hallucinations.
- [I] Without a registry check, invented PyPI names cannot be separated from real packages that simply are not installed.
- [I] Shares are given without totals, so per-answer rates cannot be worked out.
- [I] The models are old and small; some Pass@1 values are as low as 0.04% [@zhang2025llm, p. 9].
- [I] Our arXiv copy lists five authors against nine in the published version, so the content may differ [@zhang2025llm, p. 1].

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [I] Our gap report does not use this paper as evidence for any gap (G1–G5).
- [I] G3: its definition ("not in the environment") is one more example of the unshared rules for deciding what counts as a hallucinated package [@zhang2025llm, p. 6].
- [A] The authors suggest better ways to find and locate hallucinations, richer retrieval sources and multi-agent systems with tools [@zhang2025llm, p. 9; @zhang2025llm, p. 10].

### Why it matters for your research
Cite it as related work only. It shows that package hallucination is a narrow slice of code hallucination when the model writes code inside an existing project. It also gives a definitional warning: "does not exist in the environment" is not the same as "does not exist on PyPI". If you build a measurement, record these as separate outcomes.

### Connections to other papers
- [V] mirandapena2026empirical also judges missing modules against the installed environment rather than a registry [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 18].
- [V] Studies that ask models to write whole programs from a prompt find package hallucination in every model tested [@spracklen2024we, p. 7; @churilov2026range, p. 6]. [I] The different task type likely explains why it is so rare here.
- [I] Its API knowledge conflicts resemble the library member hallucinations (calls to functions a real library lacks) studied by twist2026library [@twist2026library, p. 1].

| Item | Detail |

### In plain words
Developers often describe the library they want in words ("a fast library", "a library from 2025"), or they misspell its name. This paper asks whether that everyday wording makes AI models invent libraries. It looks at two kinds of error: library name hallucinations (importing a library that does not exist) and library member hallucinations (calling a function that a real library does not have) [@twist2026library, p. 1]. The authors present it as the first systematic study of how user-level prompt wording affects these errors [@twist2026library, p. 2].

### How they did it
1. They started from BigCodeBench, a public coding benchmark, and kept 356 tasks that use 30 libraries without naming them [@twist2026library, p. 3].
2. Experiment 1 inserted descriptions mined from 3,917 library questions on the Software Recommendations StackExchange site, such as "fast" or "from 2025" [@twist2026library, p. 4].
3. Experiment 2 inserted mistakes: one-character typos, multi-character typos or fake library names, each checked to be unregistered [@twist2026library, p. 4].
4. Seven models answered each prompt three times through their providers' APIs, in a fresh session with no system prompt [@twist2026library, p. 3; @twist2026library, p. 4].
5. Python's own parser read the import lines, and names were compared with PyPI after standard name normalisation [@twist2026library, p. 4].
6. Two measures: RHR, the share of responses with a hallucination, and THR, the share of tasks where at least one of the three responses hallucinates [@twist2026library, p. 5].

- Models with exact versions: GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5-mini, Ministral-8B, Qwen-2.5-Coder 32B, Llama-3.3 70B, DeepSeek-V3.1 and Claude-4.5-Haiku, each at its default temperature (0.3 to 1.0) [@twist2026library, p. 15].

- The JavaScript and Rust study used 500 tasks and one response per task [@twist2026library, p. 20].
- LibHalluBench has 4,173 prompts and is released on Hugging Face (gated) and as a PyPI package [@twist2026library, p. 8].
- The detector was checked by hand on 200 responses [@twist2026library, p. 15].
- The date of the PyPI name list is not reported.

## An Empirical Analysis of Static Analysis Methods for Detection and Mitigation of Code Library Hallucinations
> **Takeaway:** Free code-checking tools such as Pyright catch some, but far from all, cases where AI-written Python uses library features that do not exist, and the authors put the realistic ceiling at about 77% [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 8; @mirandapena2026empirical, p. 12]. The tools check against installed packages, not PyPI, so they cannot spot a squatted package.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Clarissa Miranda-Pena, Andrew Reeson, Cécile Paris, Josiah Poon, Jonathan K. Kummerfeld |
| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
| Status | Preprint; the PDF states acceptance in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), which we have not verified |
| Identifier | arXiv 2604.07755 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2604.07755) |
| Paper type | Comparative evaluation of detection, repair and constrained decoding, with manual annotation |
| Relevance to us | Medium — RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 (main); RQ1 (partial) |

### In plain words
Static analysis means checking code without running it, a bit like a spell-checker for programs. Mypy and Pyright are free static checkers for Python. Here a library hallucination is code that would only work if imagined libraries, functions, parameters or types existed [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 3]. The paper asks three things: how many of these errors such tools catch, whether an AI can repair them using the tools' messages, and whether a grammar can stop the model from writing them in the first place [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 2].

### How they did it
1. Six models wrote code for three Python benchmarks: DS-1000, ODEX and BigCodeBench [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 5].
2. Four detectors were compared: Mypy, Pyright, a grammar built automatically from library documentation, and o3-mini as an AI judge [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 4].
3. The authors hand-annotated 600 failure cases to see what the tools could catch in principle [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 6]. Annotators agreed well, with Cohen's kappa (agreement corrected for chance) of 0.79 [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 7].
4. Repair: o3-mini fixed the code given the error alone or the error plus Mypy or Pyright output [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 9; @mirandapena2026empirical, p. 10].
5. Constrained decoding: the grammar limits which tokens the model may write, run in llama.cpp, a tool for running models locally [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 4; @mirandapena2026empirical, p. 11].

### Data and setup
- Benchmarks: DS-1000 (1,000 problems), ODEX (550 of 945 used) and BigCodeBench (1,140) [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 5].

> **Takeaway:** Before AI coding tools existed, this study of 174 real malicious packages showed that most attacks used lookalike names and most ran their harmful code the moment the package was installed [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 11; @ohm2020backstabbers, p. 12]. It explains why simply installing a hallucinated package name can be dangerous.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Authors | Marc Ohm, Henrik Plate, Arnold Sykosch, Michael Meier |
| Year · Venue | 2020 · Lecture Notes in Computer Science (proceedings chapter) |
| Status | Peer-reviewed (LNCS proceedings chapter); our copy is the arXiv version; a 2020 background paper that predates AI coding assistants |
| Identifier | DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-52683-2_2 (arXiv 2005.09535) |
| Paper type | Descriptive review: hand-curated dataset of real malicious packages plus attack trees |
| Relevance to us | Medium — RQ2 (main), RQ3 and RQ5 (background) |

### In plain words
A software supply chain attack hides malicious code in a package that other people's software depends on. Packages come from registries such as npm (JavaScript), PyPI (Python) and RubyGems (Ruby). Typosquatting means registering a name close to a popular package so that people install it by mistake. The authors collected real malicious packages from these registries, analysed them by hand and drew attack trees, diagrams of the different ways an attack can be carried out [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 1; @ohm2020backstabbers, p. 2]. Slopsquatting is a newer variant of the same attack in which an AI model, not a human typo, supplies the wrong name.

### How they did it
1. They searched the Snyk vulnerability database, security advisories and research blogs in mid-2019 and updated the search in January 2020 [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 4].
2. Registries had removed the malicious code, so they recovered it from old mirrors, internet archives and research repositories [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 4].
3. They analysed each package by hand: when it runs, under what conditions, how it got in, what it tries to do and whether it hides its code [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 4; @ohm2020backstabbers, p. 5].
4. They built two attack trees, one for getting malicious code into a dependency tree and one for running it [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 7; @ohm2020backstabbers, p. 9].
5. Results are descriptive shares and averages, with no statistical tests [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 11].

### Data and setup
- 469 malicious packages were identified, 59 proof-of-concept packages were excluded, and code was obtained for 174 [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 9].
- Code was obtained for 109 of 374 npm packages, 28 of 44 PyPI packages, 37 of 41 RubyGems packages and none of 10 Maven packages [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 9; @ohm2020backstabbers, p. 10].
- The dataset is on GitHub but shared only on justified request, for ethical reasons [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 10].
- The number of people coding the packages and their agreement are not reported.

### Key findings
- [V] 56% of packages start their malicious code at install time; on PyPI the share is 96% [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 11].
- [V] 61% used typosquatting. The mean edit distance (number of single-letter changes) to the imitated name is 2.3 [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 12].
- [V] Some reuse the exact name of a package from another repository, such as python-sqlite from the Linux apt repository [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 12].
- [V] Trojan horses, new packages with no lookalike target, are 11% overall [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 13].
- [V] Malicious packages stayed available for 209 days on average before public reporting (median 67) [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 11].
- [V] 41% run only under certain conditions, which helps them evade analysis sandboxes (isolated test environments) [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 12].
- [V] Data theft is the most common goal, at 55% [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 18]. Targets include SSH keys, npm credentials and environment variables [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 13].
- [A] A new malicious package "has to be discovered and referenced" by users before it can do harm [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 7].
- [A] The authors recommend version pinning and disabling install scripts, enforced by default [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 16].

### Limitations and weaknesses
- [A] The dataset leans towards npm, and no packages could be obtained for Java or PHP [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 18].
- [A] About 34% are droppers whose second-stage download may be gone [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 18].
- [A] The attack trees are not complete [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 4].
- [I] Only 28 PyPI packages, so PyPI shares rest on very few cases.
- [I] Only detected and retrievable attacks are included; undetected ones are missing.
- [I] Hand coding without any agreement check, and per-registry shares are read from bar charts.
- [I] The data end in 2019, before AI coding tools, and registry defences have changed since.

### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
- [V] G1: install-time execution means the install itself is the harmful event [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 11]. [I] Measuring generated text alone therefore misses the moment of harm.
- [A] G2: its user-side countermeasures (pinning, disabled install scripts) support a lightweight guard on the user's machine [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 16].
- [V] G5: packages stayed live for 209 days on average [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 11]. [I] Watching hallucinated names for six months or less can miss later abuse.
- [I] Its attack tree has no branch for discovery through AI recommendations, which is exactly the route slopsquatting uses.

### Why it matters for your research
This paper gives you the threat model. Slopsquatting is a "create new package" attack in which the AI performs the discovery step the authors saw as the attacker's main obstacle [@ohm2020backstabbers, p. 7]. Because most malicious packages run on install, a defence must act before installation. For a safe study, never install unknown packages; use read-only registry data. The typosquat edit-distance profile can help set thresholds for a lookalike check.

- [V] zheng2026when found 86.48% of invented Rust crate names within 5 edits of a real crate [@zheng2026when, p. 7], close to the typosquat distances here.
- [I] Its python-sqlite case resembles the import-name confusion that twist2026library and raj2026names handle in opposite ways [@twist2026library, p. 4; @raj2026names, p. 8].

1	### FILE: reports/reading-guide/papers/zheng2026when.md
2	```markdown
3	## When LLMs Invent Rust Crates: An Empirical Study of Hallucination Patterns and Mitigation
4	> **Takeaway:** In Rust code written by six AI models, about one in five references to a crate (a Rust package) pointed to a crate that does not exist, and model size and temperature barely changed this [@zheng2026when, p. 5; @zheng2026when, p. 6]. Almost half of these "invented crates" are mix-ups with Rust's own standard library, and part of the count may come from the authors' name parser, so treat the headline rate with care.
5	
6	| Item | Detail |
7	|---|---|
8	| Authors | Jieming Zheng, Hao Guan, Yepang Liu |
9	| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
10	| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed); a reported conference acceptance is not verified |
11	| Identifier | arXiv 2606.08444 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2606.08444) |
12	| Paper type | Measurement study plus a prompt-based mitigation experiment |
13	| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |
14	
15	### In plain words
16	Rust is a programming language. Its packages are called "crates" and are published on the registry crates.io. A package hallucination happens when an AI model names a package that does not exist. An attacker can register such an invented name and fill it with malware; this attack is called slopsquatting. Earlier studies looked at Python and JavaScript; the authors present this as the first large study for Rust [@zheng2026when, p. 1]. One caveat matters for us: in Rust, mentioning a crate in a source file does not download it [@zheng2026when, p. 1]. So this paper measures names in generated text, not what actually gets installed.
17	
18	### How they did it
19	1. They built 2,794 Rust coding tasks from three sources: 1,001 Stack Overflow questions, 793 tasks made from documented functions in popular GitHub projects, and 1,000 tasks that a Qwen model wrote from crate descriptions [@zheng2026when, p. 2; @zheng2026when, p. 3].
20	2. Each model wrote code for every task with its default settings [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
21	3. A script pulled crate names out of the code with three text patterns: use lines, path prefixes such as name::item, and extern crate lines [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
22	4. Each name was compared with a reference list: every crates.io name, plus Rust's standard and compiler crates and known aliases. Any name not on the list counted as hallucinated [@zheng2026when, p. 4; @zheng2026when, p. 5].
23	5. The main measure is the Crate Hallucination Rate (CHR): hallucinated references divided by all extracted references [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
24	6. To describe patterns they used edit distance (how many single-letter changes turn one name into another) and the overlap of invented names between models [@zheng2026when, p. 7].
25	7. They tested two prompt-based fixes on the three open models. Self-refinement asks the model to check its own crate names and regenerate up to 3 times. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) adds descriptions of 5 matching crates, drawn from the 10,000 most-downloaded, to the prompt [@zheng2026when, p. 8].
26	
27	### Data and setup
28	- 14 model variants from six families: GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Opus, Qwen2.5-Coder (0.5B to 32B), DeepSeek-Coder-V2 (16B and 236B) and OpenCoder (1.5B and 8B). "B" means billions of parameters, a rough measure of model size [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
29	- Main run: 16,764 code snippets with 48,494 extracted crate references [@zheng2026when, p. 5]. [I] That is one answer per task per model.
30	- Temperature (a setting that makes output more random) was varied from 0 to 2 on four models [@zheng2026when, p. 6].
31	- Open models were run through Ollama, a tool for running models locally, on a server with 8 RTX 6000 Ada GPUs [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
32	- Not reported: the quantization level of the Ollama models and the date of the crates.io name list.
33	- Tasks, prompts, scripts and results are shared on figshare [@zheng2026when, p. 10].
34	
35	### Key findings
36	- [V] 10,779 of 48,494 crate references were hallucinated, an overall CHR of 22.23% [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
37	- [V] Gemini 2.5 Pro had the lowest rate (16.18%) and Claude 4 Opus the highest (26.90%) [@zheng2026when, p. 5].
38	- [V] Size did not predict the rate within Qwen2.5-Coder (p = 0.912). Temperature had no significant effect (p = 0.4859), while the choice of model did (p = 0.0173) [@zheng2026when, p. 5; @zheng2026when, p. 6].
39	- [V] 45.47% of hallucinations are standard-library or internal modules treated as outside crates, led by thread and duration [@zheng2026when, p. 6].
40	- [V] The other invented names sit close to real ones: 40.78% are 1–2 edits from a real crate and 86.48% within 5; 32.96% drop a hyphen that the real crate has [@zheng2026when, p. 7].
41	- [V] 38.9% of frequently invented names are borrowed from other ecosystems, such as queryparser from Python [@zheng2026when, p. 8].
42	- [V] Self-refinement lowered the rate by 2.22–3.26 points. RAG lowered it by 1.92 and 0.96 points for two models and raised it by 0.34 for Qwen2.5-Coder [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
43	
44	### Limitations and weaknesses
45	- [A] Whether invented crates would be installed, break builds or be exploitable was not measured [@zheng2026when, p. 10].
46	- [A] Alias coverage is incomplete, so the true rate is "likely slightly lower" [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
47	- [A] A third of the tasks were written by a Qwen model, and models change fast [@zheng2026when, p. 10].
48	- [I] The path-prefix pattern may also catch type names such as Duration::from_secs. Odd top-10 names such as trefcell and tu32 look like a parser bug that the paper does not discuss [@zheng2026when, p. 6].
49	- [I] The counts do not match: 10,779 hallucinated references in one section, 13,332 non-module occurrences in the next [@zheng2026when, p. 5; @zheng2026when, p. 7].
50	- [I] The abstract claims "surprisingly consistent" rates and no loss of code quality, but the model effect is significant and code quality was never measured [@zheng2026when, p. 1; @zheng2026when, p. 6].
51	- [I] The paper does not say how hyphens in crate names were matched to underscores in code, which affects the 32.96% hyphen finding.
52	- [I] Ollama's default downloads are usually quantized, which may blur size comparisons. One answer per task and no confidence intervals.
53	
54	### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
55	- [A] G1: installation through Cargo, Rust's package tool, was not measured [@zheng2026when, p. 10]. What models actually install remains open.
56	- [A] G2: the authors propose a Rust-aware guard that separates standard modules from outside crates, checks near-miss names against the registry and cross-checks the project's Cargo.toml file, but they do not test it [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
57	- [I] G3: its unit (every source-level reference, including standard-library mix-ups) differs from other papers' units, so 22% cannot be compared directly with Python or JavaScript rates [@zheng2026when, p. 4].
58	- [I] G4: the unreported quantization of the Ollama models is a hidden confound.
59	- [A] The prompt fixes still need testing on commercial models [@zheng2026when, p. 9].
60	
61	### Why it matters for your research
62	This is the only Rust study in the set. Its main lesson is about measurement: the reference list and the parser decide much of the rate, so hand-check a sample of flagged names in any study of your own. The near-miss pattern (most invented names are a few letters from a real one) supports adding a lookalike check to a pre-install guard. The small Qwen2.5-Coder models it used run on a laptop through Ollama, and its data are public, so a partial replication is cheap.
63	
64	### Connections to other papers
65	- [V] Temperature: spracklen2024we found rates rising sharply above temperature 1 [@spracklen2024we, p. 8]; here there was no effect for Rust (evidence matrix contradiction 4).
66	- [V] Size: krishna2025importing found that larger models hallucinate less [@krishna2025importing, p. 6]; no size effect here (contradiction 3).
67	- [V] RAG cut Python rates sharply in spracklen2024we [@spracklen2024we, p. 13] but helped little here (contradiction 6).
68	- [I] spracklen2024we reported that 48.6% of invented Python names are 6 or more edits from a real one [@spracklen2024we, p. 11]. This paper counts occurrences rather than names, so the two figures are not directly comparable.
69	- [V] When the fake name is planted in the prompt, dasu2026refusing finds nonexistent Rust crates fabricated on 87% of prompts [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8]. That measures accepting a name, not inventing one.
70	```

72	### FILE: reports/reading-guide/papers/dasu2026refusing.md
73	```markdown
74	## Refusing the Impossible: A Taxonomy and Benchmark for Code Hallucination in Large Language Models
75	> **Takeaway:** When a coding request names a package that does not exist, open AI models usually write code for it instead of saying it does not exist, and bigger models barely do better on this [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6; @dasu2026refusing, p. 8]. The fake name is written into the prompt, so this paper measures how often models accept a planted name, not how often they invent one.
76	
77	| Item | Detail |
78	|---|---|
79	| Authors | Vishnu Asutosh Dasu, Ashish Kundu, Gang Tan |
80	| Year · Venue | 2026 · arXiv |
81	| Status | Preprint (not peer-reviewed) |
82	| Identifier | arXiv 2609.03267 (DOI 10.48550/arxiv.2609.03267) |
83	| Paper type | Benchmark and evaluation study with an AI judge checked against human labels |
84	| Relevance to us | High — RQ1, RQ2, RQ3, RQ4, RQ5 |
85	
86	### In plain words
87	Most coding benchmarks contain only tasks that can be solved. This paper asks what happens when a request cannot be satisfied, for example because it names a package that does not exist or asks for an impossible algorithm. The right answer is to refuse [@dasu2026refusing, p. 1]. The authors call code built on something that does not exist "code hallucination", sort these failures into a taxonomy (a structured list of types), and release a benchmark to test them [@dasu2026refusing, p. 1]. Matched solvable tasks check that a model is not simply refusing everything.
88	
89	### How they did it
90	1. They hand-wrote 270 unsatisfiable requests in 24 subcategories. One family covers plausible but nonexistent things, such as packages on PyPI, npm, crates.io and Go, Java APIs and C headers [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
91	2. Each request comes with a note naming the planted fake item, for example a crate called serde_ultra [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
92	3. They added 91 solvable control tasks that differ only slightly from the fake ones [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
93	4. Requests cover six programming languages and ten "framings", such as internal documentation or a learner's question [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
94	5. 17 open-weight models (models whose weights can be downloaded) each answered once at temperature 0, the least random setting [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
95	6. Claude Opus 4.6 acted as judge with a fixed rubric, labelling each answer as correct, hallucination or refusal [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
96	7. The judge was checked against 138 human labels, and results carry 95% bootstrap intervals (ranges of likely values found by resampling the prompts) [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
97	
98	### Data and setup
99	- 6,137 judged responses from 17 models with 6.7B to 671B parameters [@dasu2026refusing, p. 1].
100	- Models up to 32B ran with 4-bit quantization (weights stored with fewer bits to save memory); larger ones ran at full precision [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
101	- The package subsets are small: twelve nonexistent npm prompts and ten nonexistent crate prompts [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9].
102	- Judge agreement with humans: 94% on outcomes, Cohen's kappa 0.91 (an agreement score corrected for chance, where 1 is perfect) [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
103	- Inference software and hardware are not reported. Code and prompts are released [@dasu2026refusing, p. 2].
104	
105	### Key findings
106	- [V] Models wrote ungrounded code for 54% of unsatisfiable requests and refused 31% [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5]. Only 1 of 1,547 control answers was a wrongful refusal [@dasu2026refusing, p. 2].
107	- [V] Scale helps with impossible tasks (hallucination 0.84 for small models, 0.32 for the largest) but much less with nonexistent things (0.88 to 0.61), and least with fake npm packages and Rust crates (1.00 to 0.85) [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6].
108	- [V] DeepSeek-V3.2 (671B) and gpt-oss 120B fabricated code for every nonexistent npm and crate prompt [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6].
109	- [V] By ecosystem, nonexistent npm packages were fabricated on 94% of prompts, Rust crates 87%, Go modules and PyPI modules 63% each, and Java APIs 33% [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
110	- [V] A misspelled real package name led to fabrication on only 14% of prompts, against 94% for a correctly spelled fake one [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
111	- [V] 66% of hallucinations were confident fabrications without any caveat [@dasu2026refusing, p. 6].
112	- [V] Wording matters more than the model: prompt identity explains 34% of outcome variation against 15% for model identity [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
113	- [V] One model suggested pip install pywfm, a name that already exists on PyPI as an unrelated 2015 package [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9].
114	
115	### Limitations and weaknesses
116	- [A] Template prompts may differ from what developers type, so absolute rates belong to this benchmark [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
117	- [A] One answer per prompt; the judge sees the note on the fake item, and the human gold set was labelled by one author [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
118	- [A] Model size is confounded with 4-bit quantization, and closed models were not tested [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
119	- [I] The user supplies the fake name, so rates such as 94% are not comparable with spontaneous invention rates from other studies.
120	- [I] Package results rest on 22 prompts per model, so per-model package rates are uncertain.
121	- [I] The judge agreed with humans on only 67% of behaviour labels, so behaviour shares are indicative [@dasu2026refusing, p. 5].
122	- [I] Publishing the fake names lets anyone register them, which could change the ground truth for future replications.
123	
124	### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
125	- [A] G1: closed frontier models and agentic settings are not evaluated [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10].
126	- [A] G2: the authors recommend checking package names against registries at generation time but do not test it [@dasu2026refusing, p. 9].
127	- [A] G4: size is confounded with quantization [@dasu2026refusing, p. 10]. The gap report lists this as a hidden confound across studies.
128	- [I] Typo amplification was dropped as a gap in our gap report because this paper and twist2026library already measure it [@dasu2026refusing, p. 8].
129	
130	### Why it matters for your research
131	This is the clearest evidence that larger models do not fix fake-package acceptance. Its benchmark is small and public, and its small models already ran at 4-bit, the setting a laptop uses. A laptop study could re-run the npm, crate and PyPI subsets on local 7B models and test whether a simple registry check before installing reduces harm. Two design habits are worth copying: matched solvable controls and an AI judge validated against human labels.
132	
133	### Connections to other papers
134	- [V] twist2026library finds the same acceptance of fake names, up to 99.22% of tasks [@twist2026library, p. 6], as does djire2026evaluating [@djire2026evaluating, p. 9].
135	- [V] twist2026library reports one-character typos accepted in up to 25.86% of tasks [@twist2026library, p. 6]. Here a typo that the model corrects counts as correct, which may explain the lower 14% [@dasu2026refusing, p. 4].
136	- [I] On model size, krishna2025importing finds a size effect [@krishna2025importing, p. 6] and zheng2026when none [@zheng2026when, p. 5]. The quantization confound here shows why size results disagree (evidence matrix contradiction 3).
137	- [V] The pywfm case is a real-world example of what spracklen2024we warns: a plain existence check passes names that are already registered [@spracklen2024we, p. 12].
138	```

140	### FILE: reports/reading-guide/papers/zhang2025llm.md
141	```markdown
142	## LLM Hallucinations in Practical Code Generation: Phenomena, Mechanism, and Mitigation
143	> **Takeaway:** In realistic Python tasks set inside real projects, most AI coding mistakes come from misunderstanding the task, and problems with missing packages make up under 1% of hallucinations [@zhang2025llm, p. 4; @zhang2025llm, p. 6]. Read it as background: it maps the kinds of code hallucination, but it does not measure invented PyPI packages.
144	
145	| Item | Detail |
146	|---|---|
147	| Authors | Ziyao Zhang, Chong Wang, Yanlin Wang, Ensheng Shi, Yuchi Ma, Wanjun Zhong, Jiachi Chen, Mingzhi Mao, Zibin Zheng (published version; our arXiv copy lists five authors) |
148	| Year · Venue | 2025 · Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering (PACMSE), ISSTA 2025 issue |
149	| Status | Peer-reviewed (PACMSE / ISSTA 2025); our copy is the arXiv version |
150	| Identifier | DOI 10.1145/3728894 (arXiv 2409.20550) |
151	| Paper type | Empirical study: hand-built taxonomy of errors plus a small mitigation pilot |
152	| Relevance to us | Low — RQ1 (marginal), RQ3 and RQ4 (background) |
153	
154	### In plain words
155	Many studies test AI coding on small, self-contained functions. This paper uses repository-level tasks instead: the model must write a function that fits into a real project with its own files and dependencies [@zhang2025llm, p. 1]. The authors read thousands of generated snippets and sorted the mistakes into a taxonomy (a structured list of error types) [@zhang2025llm, p. 3; @zhang2025llm, p. 4]. Package hallucination is only one small corner of that map. The paper is useful to us mainly for context and for a warning about definitions.
156	
157	### How they did it
158	1. They used CoderEval Python, a benchmark of 230 tasks taken from real projects, each with tests and a working project environment [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
159	2. Six models produced 10 answers per task with nucleus sampling at temperature 0.6, a moderately random setting [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
160	3. Two authors open-coded (read examples and created labels from what they saw) 1,380 snippets from 23 tasks to build the first version of the taxonomy [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
161	4. Three volunteers labelled the remaining snippets, and one author reviewed all labels [@zhang2025llm, p. 3; @zhang2025llm, p. 10].
162	5. They compared models and proposed root causes [@zhang2025llm, p. 8].
163	6. A pilot fix used RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): it added the 10 most similar code snippets from the same project to the prompt. Success was measured by Pass@1, the share of tasks where the first answer passes the tests [@zhang2025llm, p. 9].
164	
165	### Data and setup
166	- Models: GPT-3.5-Turbo, CodeGen-350M, PanGu-alpha-2.6B, DeepSeekCoder-6.7B, CodeLlama-7B-Python and StarCoder2-7B [@zhang2025llm, p. 3].
167	- [I] 230 tasks × 6 models × 10 answers gives 13,800 snippets by our arithmetic; the paper does not state the total number of hallucinations.
168	- A "non-existent package" means one that is not available in the task's environment [@zhang2025llm, p. 6]. There is no check against PyPI.
169	- Code, data and results are on GitHub [@zhang2025llm, p. 1]. Hardware and exact prompts are not reported.
170	
171	### Key findings
172	- [V] Three categories: task requirement conflicts 43.53%, factual knowledge conflicts 31.91% and project context conflicts 24.56% of hallucinations [@zhang2025llm, p. 4; @zhang2025llm, p. 5; @zhang2025llm, p. 6].
173	- [V] Environment conflicts, which include importing a package missing from the environment, are only 0.94%. The example is a package called _lfu_cache [@zhang2025llm, p. 6].
174	- [I] _lfu_cache is not a valid PyPI distribution name, so it is probably a missing internal module. The 0.94% is therefore an upper bound on invented-package cases.
175	- [V] API knowledge conflicts are much more common (20.41%), for example a parameter that a real function does not have, as in timedelta(year=1) [@zhang2025llm, p. 6].
176	- [V] Library knowledge conflicts make up 2.68% [@zhang2025llm, p. 5].
177	- [V] One security-relevant example: generated code used yaml.load instead of the safer safe_load [@zhang2025llm, p. 5].
178	- [V] Task requirement conflicts are the most frequent category for all six models [@zhang2025llm, p. 8].
179	- [V] RAG raised Pass@1 for every model, for example ChatGPT from 10.40% to 12.61% and CodeLlama from 2.17% to 5.22%. [A] The authors call the gain modest [@zhang2025llm, p. 9].
180	
181	### Limitations and weaknesses
182	- [A] Python only and only 230 tasks [@zhang2025llm, p. 10].
183	- [A] No formal inter-rater reliability measure (a statistic for how far independent labellers agree) [@zhang2025llm, p. 10].
184	- [I] The fix was judged by Pass@1, not by counting hallucinations, so it does not show that RAG reduces hallucinations.
185	- [I] Without a registry check, invented PyPI names cannot be separated from real packages that simply are not installed.
186	- [I] Shares are given without totals, so per-answer rates cannot be worked out.
187	- [I] The models are old and small; some Pass@1 values are as low as 0.04% [@zhang2025llm, p. 9].
188	- [I] Our arXiv copy lists five authors against nine in the published version, so the content may differ [@zhang2025llm, p. 1].
189	
190	### Gaps and future work this paper leaves open
191	- [I] Our gap report does not use this paper as evidence for any gap (G1–G5).
192	- [I] G3: its definition ("not in the environment") is one more example of the unshared rules for deciding what counts as a hallucinated package [@zhang2025llm, p. 6].
193	- [A] The authors suggest better ways to find and locate hallucinations, richer retrieval sources and multi-agent systems with tools [@zhang2025llm, p. 9; @zhang2025llm, p. 10].
194	
195	### Why it matters for your research
196	Cite it as related work only. It shows that package hallucination is a narrow slice of code hallucination when the model writes code inside an existing project. It also gives a definitional warning: "does not exist in the environment" is not the same as "does not exist on PyPI". If you build a measurement, record these as separate outcomes.
197	
198	### Connections to other papers
199	- [V] mirandapena2026empirical also judges missing modules against the installed environment rather than a registry [@mirandapena2026empirical, p. 18].
200	- [V] Studies that ask models to write whole programs from a prompt find package hallucination in every model tested [@spracklen2024we, p. 7; @churilov2026range, p. 6]. [I] The different task type likely explains why it is so rare here.
201	- [I] Its API knowledge conflicts resemble the library member hallucinations (calls to functions a real library lacks) studied by twist2026library [@twist2026library, p. 1].
202	```
